anchor_text: Now is the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer by this sun of York
summary: Richard opens with an extended metaphor: the Yorkist wars (winter, clouds, storms) have been replaced by peace (summer) now that his brother Edward IV of the house of York sits securely on the throne. 'Sun of York' puns on both the sun as a symbol of royalty and on 'son' — Edward is both the sunlight and the son of the house of York. The speech turns abruptly at line 14 ('But I') when Richard reveals he cannot enjoy this peace.
detail: The sun emblem is also an Yorkist heraldic badge — the 'sun in splendour' was a device of Edward IV, making 'sun of York' an exact political compliment as well as a metaphor. The opening sentence runs fourteen lines, a sustained periodic construction that mimics the release of long tension only to snap into Richard's bitter counter-statement at 'But I.' The structure — peace celebrated, then immediately subverted — establishes the soliloquy as a statement of intent: the audience is let in on the plan before the play begins.

sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'discontent'; 'sun' (punning on 'son').

Onions and the Hammond 1981 Arden edition (Methuen) are both real, standard scholarly references that support the sun/son pun and the rhetorical structure described.

The sun/son pun, the Yorkist heraldic 'sun in splendour' badge for Edward IV, and the fourteen-line periodic sentence capped by the pivot at 'But I' are all mainstream, well-documented readings with no overreach.

anchor_text: our brows bound with victorious wreaths; / Our bruised arms hung up for monuments
summary: After a Roman or medieval victory, soldiers hung their armor and weapons in temples or great halls as trophies ('monuments'), signaling the end of fighting. 'Brows bound with victorious wreaths' echoes the Roman tradition of crowning victors with laurel. Both images mark the transition from a state of war to civic celebration that Richard is about to lament.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'monument' (a trophy or memorial of war).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 5
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902) is a real reference work; s.v. 'monument' supporting the trophy/memorial-of-war gloss is consistent with the entry.
The Roman victor's laurel wreath and the practice of hanging captured arms as trophies are straightforwardly attested and accurately applied to these lines.

anchor_text: Our stern alarums chang'd to merry meetings, / Our dreadful marches to delightful measures
summary: 'Alarums' are military trumpet calls signaling battle or attack — the Elizabethan stage direction 'alarum' means a call to arms, the noise of combat. 'Measures' are formal dances. Richard is contrasting the sounds of war (battle-trumpets and marching armies) with the sounds of peace (festive music and dancing). Both words are obsolete in these senses today.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'alarum' (a military call to arms); 'measure' (a stately dance).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 7
Onions s.v. 'alarum' (military call to arms) and 'measure' (a stately dance) are standard, well-attested entries that directly support the archaic-vocab gloss.
'Alarum' as a military trumpet call and 'measure' as a formal dance are standard Elizabethan usages accurately glossed here.

anchor_text: mounting barbed steeds / To fright the souls of fearful adversaries
summary: 'Barbed steeds' are war-horses armored with 'barbs' (also 'bards') — metal plates or padded coverings fitted over a horse's chest, flanks, and head as protection. The word is a corruption of 'barded,' from Old French 'barde' (horse-armor). Charging cavalry in such barding was among the most terrifying sights of medieval warfare. Richard is remembering the era of armored knightly combat that peace has now made obsolete.

anchor_text: I,--that am not shap'd for sportive tricks, / Nor made to court an amorous looking-glass
summary: Richard delivers a self-description built on a triple anaphora ('I, that... / I, that... / I, that...') emphasizing his physical deformity as the reason he cannot participate in the pleasures of peacetime — flirtation, vanity, gallantry. 'Court an amorous looking-glass' means to admire himself in a mirror the way a vain lover would; 'sportive tricks' means romantic or sexual games. Richard presents his deformity as the cause of his villainy, a self-pitying logic the play will repeatedly test.
detail: The anaphora is a standard rhetorical figure (repetition of the same phrase at the start of successive clauses), but Shakespeare uses it here to accumulate a crescendo of self-exclusion that ends with the blunt declaration 'I am determined to prove a villain' (TLN 30). The word 'determined' carries both the modern sense (resolved) and a Calvinist overtone (decreed by fate or nature) — Richard hints he was born to this role, not merely choosing it.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'sportive' (amorous, wanton); 'determined' (fixed, resolved; also fated).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 14
Onions s.v. 'sportive' (amorous, wanton) and 'determined' (fixed; also fated) are real entries and directly support the lexical and rhetorical claims made.

The anaphora reading is sound, but calling 'determined' a 'Calvinist overtone' is an overreach: the word's primary senses here are 'resolved' and 'fated by nature/constitution', and imposing specifically Calvinist predestination theology onto a generic Elizabethan use of the word goes beyond what the text requires — the claim needs qualification to 'medium' confidence.

anchor_text: I, that am curtail'd of this fair proportion, / Cheated of feature by dissembling nature
summary: Richard calls himself 'curtail'd' (cut short, deprived) of normal bodily proportion and 'cheated of feature' — that is, denied a well-made face and form by a nature that 'dissembled' (disguised its intention or deceived him). This draws on the tradition, derived from Thomas More's History of Richard III and carried into Holinshed, that Richard was born deformed — with a hunched back, withered arm, and unequal shoulders. More says he was 'ill-featured of limbes, croke-backed.
detail: ' The 2012 discovery of Richard's skeleton confirmed scoliosis but not the extreme deformity More and Shakespeare describe. More's hostile Tudor account is the primary literary source for this portrait; More had it from Cardinal Morton, Richard's enemy, so the deformity is political caricature as much as biography. The word 'dissembling' is precise: nature is itself a hypocrite, promising the full human form but delivering a flawed copy — a neat parallel to Richard's own dissembling, and a way of projecting his hypocrisy onto the universe that made him.

sources.name: More, History of King Richard III
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (written c. 1513-18; printed 1557), description of Richard's body.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), reproducing More's physical description of Richard.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 18
More's History of Richard III (c. 1513–18) does describe Richard as 'ill featured of limbs, crook-backed'; Holinshed 1587 reproduces this description, and both citations are accurate.

The Tudor chronicle tradition from More and Holinshed as source for Richard's deformity is accurately stated; the note about the 2012 skeleton confirming scoliosis but not extreme deformity is a responsible qualification; the 'dissembling' reading is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: this weak piping time of peace
summary: 'Piping time of peace' means a time when pipes (flutes, recorders, the shepherd's pipe) are played — the music of pastoral ease and celebration rather than of military drums and trumpets. 'Weak' is Richard's contemptuous judgment on peace itself: for him the martial era was strong, peace is feeble. The phrase condenses his personality into five words.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'pipe' (a wind instrument; piping = playing a pipe, hence festive or pastoral).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 24
Onions s.v. 'pipe' supports the pastoral/festive sense of 'piping' and directly underpins the archaic-vocab gloss.
The pipe as a pastoral/festive instrument contrasted with military drums, and 'weak' as Richard's contemptuous valuation of peace, are soundly grounded in the text and standard commentary.

anchor_text: I am determined to prove a villain, / And hate the idle pleasures of these days
summary: This is the explicit statement of Richard's program, delivered directly to the audience. He adopts the posture of the stage Machiavel — the villain who announces his plot with gleeful frankness, confident the audience will enjoy the game — and the older morality-play Vice, the comic tempter who confides his deceits to the crowd. Both theatrical traditions gave Elizabethan audiences a framework for receiving a self-announced villain as an entertainer rather than simply a monster.
detail: The Stage Machiavel (named for Niccolo Machiavelli, whose Prince was read as a manual for amoral scheming) was a stock Elizabethan figure: Richard claims in 3 Henry VI 3.2 to set 'the murderous Machiavel to school.' The Vice of morality drama was a jester-tempter who winks at the audience while leading the hero into sin. Richard combines both: he is clever, funny, and horrifying at once, and his self-declared villainy is framed as virtuoso performance, not confession.

sources.name: Spivack, Shakespeare and the Allegory of Evil
sources.citation: Spivack, B. (1958). Shakespeare and the Allegory of Evil. Columbia UP (on the Vice tradition).

sources.name: Machiavelli, The Prince
sources.citation: Niccolo Machiavelli, Il Principe (written 1513, printed 1532); the Elizabethan stage villain built on caricature of this text.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 30

Spivack's Shakespeare and the Allegory of Evil (Columbia UP, 1958) is a real and foundational work on the Vice tradition; Machiavelli's Il Principe dates of composition (1513) and first printing (1532) are accurate.

The Vice/stage Machiavel dual inheritance for Richard's self-announced villainy is mainstream scholarship (Spivack, Rossiter) and both the 3H6 3.2 Machiavel line and the morality-play Vice framework are well-attested; no overreach.

anchor_text: Plots have I laid, inductions dangerous
summary: 'Inductions' here does not mean introductions in the modern sense; it means preparatory steps, preliminary measures that lead into or bring about something larger — specifically, the beginning moves of a dangerous scheme. The word is used with quiet theatrical self-awareness: an 'induction' was also the opening act of a play, and Richard thinks of his scheming as staging a performance.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'induction' (a leading in; a preparatory step; also the introductory scene of a play).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 32
Onions s.v. 'induction' (a leading-in; preparatory step; also the introductory scene of a play) is a real entry that directly supports both senses claimed.

Both the archaic sense of 'inductions' (preliminary steps) and the meta-theatrical secondary sense (opening act of a play) are documented in Onions and are appropriate here; the theatrical self-awareness reading is mainstream.

anchor_text: should Clarence closely be mew'd up,-- / About a prophecy which says that G / Of Edward's heirs the murderer shall be
summary: 'Mew'd up' means shut in or caged — a 'mew' was a cage for hawks while they moulted. The prophecy that the letter 'G' would murder the king's heirs is a real element of the Tudor chronicle tradition. King Edward IV, already suspicious and unstable, fixes on George (Clarence's first name) as the 'G'; Richard, whose title Gloucester also begins with G, is the real threat he cannot see. This ironic misdirection — Richard plants the prophecy knowing it will destroy his brother while concealing his own guilt — is the play's first demonstration of his method.
detail: Holinshed (following More) records this prophecy and Edward's superstitious reliance on it; More presents Edward as a credulous, sickly king manipulated by Richard. The prophecy mechanism shows Richard as the puppet-master of information: he engineers the very fear that destroys Clarence. The audience, having just heard his plan in soliloquy, sees the trap springing in real time.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the prophecy of 'G' and the imprisonment of Clarence.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'mew' (a cage or enclosure for hawks; to cage).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 38
Holinshed (following More) does record the 'G' prophecy and Edward's imprisonment of Clarence; Onions s.v. 'mew' (cage for hawks; to cage) is standard — both citations are accurate and supportive.

The hawking origin of 'mew'd up' is correct, the 'G' prophecy in Holinshed/More is accurate, and the reading of Richard as the unseen second 'G' (Gloucester) who is the real murderer is the standard ironic interpretation of the scene.

anchor_text: from the cross-row plucks the letter G, / And says a wizard told him that by G / His issue disinherited should be
summary: The 'cross-row' (also called the cross-and-row or Christ-cross row) was the alphabet as printed in Elizabethan hornbooks and primers, so called because it was headed by a cross. To 'pluck the letter G from the cross-row' means to take out just that one letter from the alphabet — a way of describing the king's obsessive focus on a single initial as the key to a prophecy. The word 'wizard' means a man who claims occult knowledge (a seer or magician, not necessarily female as 'witch' often was).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cross-row' (the alphabet, from the cross prefixed to it in early hornbooks and primers; also 'Christ-cross-row').

'Cross-row' as the hornbook alphabet headed by a cross, and 'wizard' as a male seer or soothsayer, are accurately glossed and directly supported by the OED; no overreach.

anchor_text: My Lady Grey his wife, Clarence, 'tis she / That tempers him to this extremity
summary: Richard contemptuously calls Queen Elizabeth by her former married name, 'Lady Grey' — Elizabeth Woodville was the widow of Sir John Grey when Edward IV married her in 1464. Using her old title instead of her royal one is a deliberate insult, a way of denying her legitimate queenship and marking her as a social inferior who married above her station. Elizabeth's Woodville family ('the queen's kindred') were widely resented by the old nobility for their rapid rise to power after the marriage.
detail: The Woodvilles' sudden ennoblement was a genuine grievance in the political history of Edward IV's reign; Holinshed and More both note the hostility the family provoked. Richard's tactic of calling Elizabeth 'Lady Grey' recurs throughout the play as a way of delegitimizing both her and her children's claim to the throne — a logic that eventually feeds into the argument that the princes are illegitimate. The line also establishes misogyny as a consistent rhetorical weapon in Richard's armory.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Elizabeth Woodville, Edward IV's queen, formerly Lady Grey.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 66
Holinshed covers Elizabeth Woodville as Edward IV's queen; the historical facts (widow of Sir John Grey, married Edward 1464, Woodville resentment) are accurate and well-sourced.

Using 'Lady Grey' rather than 'Queen Elizabeth' as a deliberate insult denying her royal status is the standard reading, historically grounded in Elizabeth Woodville's background and the nobles' resentment of the Woodvilles.

anchor_text: night-walking heralds / That trudge betwixt the king and Mistress Shore
summary: Jane Shore (died c. 1527) was the most famous mistress of King Edward IV — a London goldsmith's wife whom the king took as his lover, known for using her influence at court generously on behalf of petitioners. 'Night-walking heralds' who carry messages between the king and Mistress Shore are go-betweens for the king's affairs. After Edward's death Richard famously accused Lord Hastings of consorting with her as part of the trumped-up treason charge he used to destroy Hastings in Act 3.
detail: Thomas More wrote a vivid biographical sketch of Jane Shore in his History of Richard III, presenting her sympathetically as a good-natured woman who used her position to help people and was later reduced to penury and public penance by Richard's malice. She is the play's emblem of Edward IV's self-indulgence and of the way Richard weaponizes sexual conduct as political accusation. Richard's dismissal of her here ('a pretty foot, / A cherry lip, a bonny eye') anticipates his later use of her name to destroy Hastings.

sources.name: More, History of King Richard III
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (c. 1513-18), on Jane Shore's biography and her role at Edward IV's court.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 74
More's History of Richard III does contain a vivid sympathetic biographical sketch of Jane Shore; her death date of c. 1527 is confirmed by multiple sources.
Jane Shore as Edward IV's mistress, More's sympathetic account, her later use by Richard against Hastings, and the summary of her historical role are all accurate and appropriately measured.

anchor_text: Naught to do with Mistress Shore! I tell thee, fellow, / He that doth naught with her, excepting one, / Were best to do it secretly alone
summary: Brakenbury says he has 'naught to do' with Mistress Shore — meaning nothing to do with her, no involvement. Richard pounces on the double meaning: 'naught' (nothing) also meant sexual intercourse in Elizabethan slang ('doing naught' = copulating). He twists the remark into a smutty joke: the only person who should be 'doing naught' with her (in either sense) is her husband — and he should do it in private. The wordplay allows Richard to mock Brakenbury, the king, and Jane Shore simultaneously while appearing to speak innocently.

sources.name: Partridge, Shakespeare's Bawdy
sources.citation: Partridge, Eric, Shakespeare's Bawdy (1947), s.v. 'naught' (sexually wanton; to do naught = to have sexual intercourse).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 100
Partridge's Shakespeare's Bawdy (1947) is a real, published reference and does gloss 'naught' as sexually wanton/to do naught = copulate, directly supporting the bawdy-pun annotation.

The 'naught' bawdy pun (nothing / sexual intercourse) is well-attested in Partridge and the wordplay on Brakenbury's innocent phrase is a correct reading; the identification of 'excepting one' as the husband (confirmed by TLN 104) is textually secure.

anchor_text: We are the queen's abjects and must obey
summary: 'Abjects' (not 'subjects') is a biting pun: a 'subject' owes loyal service to a sovereign, but Richard substitutes 'abjects' — those who are cast down, humiliated, treated as worthless. He is mocking the idea that the queen effectively commands the nobles, implying they are reduced from proud lords to her discarded inferiors. The pun is also a barely concealed insult to Brakenbury, who is enforcing the queen's will.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'abject' n. (one who is cast down or degraded; a person of the lowest condition). Compare Psalm 35:15 (Geneva 1599) 'the abjects.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 108
OED s.v. 'abject' n. (one cast down, of the lowest condition) is a real entry; the Geneva Bible 1599 Psalm 35:15 does use the word 'abjects,' confirming the biblical parallel cited.
'Abjects' as a pun on 'subjects' (those cast down / degraded vs loyal subordinates) is the standard gloss for this line and the OED sense is correctly applied.

anchor_text: Go tread the path that thou shalt ne'er return. / Simple, plain Clarence!--I do love thee so / That I will shortly send thy soul to heaven
summary: As soon as Clarence is out of hearing, Richard drops his mask. The three lines are a miniature aside — a theatrical convention where a character speaks directly to the audience while remaining inaudible to others on stage. Richard's affectionate words to Clarence's face ('I will perform it to enfranchise you,' TLN 112) reverse instantly into a murder plan. The word 'Simple' means naive or gullible, not dim-witted; Richard is contemptuous of his brother's trust in him. This switch — warmth in public, cold calculation in private — is the structural rhythm of his character throughout the play.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'simple' (guileless, not cunning, easily deceived).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 120
Onions s.v. 'simple' (guileless, easily deceived) is a real entry that directly supports the gloss; the rhetorical observation about the aside requires no separate source.

The aside convention, the reversal of Richard's feigned affection the moment Clarence exits, and 'Simple' as 'guileless/naive' rather than 'dim' are all soundly grounded in the text and standard Onions usage.

anchor_text: the eagles should be mew'd / Whiles kites and buzzards prey at liberty
summary: Hastings uses a bird-of-prey metaphor for the political situation: eagles (noble, legitimate lords like Clarence and himself) are caged ('mew'd' — see note at TLN 38), while kites and buzzards (lesser, scavenging birds — a figure for the upstart Woodvilles and their allies) fly free and prey at will. In Elizabethan natural history the eagle was the king of birds, a figure for nobility and royalty; kites and buzzards were contemptible scavengers. The imagery reflects the aristocratic resentment of the queen's family.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'mew' (to shut in, to cage); 'kite' (a bird of prey; fig. a rapacious person).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 135
Onions s.v. 'mew' (to cage) and 'kite' (rapacious scavenging bird; fig. a rapacious person) are real entries that directly support the bird-of-prey metaphor gloss.

The bird hierarchy — eagles as noble lords, kites and buzzards as contemptible scavengers figuring the upstart Woodvilles — is a standard Elizabethan natural-history and heraldic reading, and 'mew'd' is correctly cross-referenced to TLN 38.

anchor_text: Now, by Saint Paul, that news is bad indeed
summary: Richard swears characteristically 'by Saint Paul' — this is his repeated oath throughout the play (cf. 3.1, 3.4). St Paul's Cathedral in London was the civic and commercial heart of the city; swearing by Saint Paul was a London citizen's oath. More pointedly, More and Holinshed's Richard is marked by conspicuous, hypocritical piety — he is always making a show of religious observance while plotting murder. The oath hints at this quality of public devotion as self-advertisement.

sources.name: More, History of King Richard III
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (c. 1513-18), on Richard's theatrical displays of religious devotion.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Richard III's public piety.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 141

More's History and Holinshed do both characterize Richard's public displays of religious devotion as theatrical and hypocritical, supporting the annotation's historical claim about his 'Saint Paul' oath.

While Richard does repeatedly swear 'by Saint Paul' and More/Holinshed do describe his hypocritical piety, the gloss conflates the oath's London-civic resonance with a separate interpretive claim about theatrical religious self-advertisement; the latter is a reasonable but secondary inference that the text alone does not securely support, and the medium confidence assigned is appropriate but the annotation stretches its evidence.

anchor_text: I'll marry Warwick's youngest daughter: / What though I kill'd her husband and her father
summary: Lady Anne Neville is the daughter of Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick ('the Kingmaker'), the most powerful noble of the Wars of the Roses, and the widow of Edward of Westminster, the Lancastrian Prince of Wales. Richard killed both her father-in-law King Henry VI and her husband Edward in battle (or at least was present at their deaths). His plan to woo her — which he pursues over Henry VI's corpse in the very next scene — is presented here as pure calculation: he wants her lands and Neville dynastic connections, not her person.

anchor_text: But yet I run before my horse to market: / Clarence still breathes; Edward still lives and reigns
summary: 'I run before my horse to market' is an Elizabethan proverb meaning to get ahead of oneself, to count one's gains before the work is done — equivalent to modern 'counting your chickens before they hatch.' Richard catches himself fantasizing about marrying Anne and reaching the crown before he has even cleared the way by killing Clarence and waiting for Edward to die. The final rhyming couplet ('count my gains') signals the end of the soliloquy, a common theatrical device for closing a scene.

anchor_text: obsequiously lament
summary: 'Obsequiously' here means 'in the manner of obsequies' — that is, as a funeral rite or mourning duty. Anne is not being servile; she is performing the ceremonies proper to the dead. An 'obsequy' (from Latin obsequium, dutiful service) was an early modern term for a funeral rite.
detail: The word is unrelated to the modern sense 'servilely.' Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'obsequious') gives the primary meaning for Shakespeare as 'pertaining to obsequies, pertaining to funeral rites.' The line establishes that Anne regards mourning Henry as a sacred obligation, not mere grief.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'obsequious'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 168
Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference work and does give the primary Shakespeare sense of 'obsequious' as pertaining to funeral rites/obsequies.
The archaic sense of 'obsequiously' as 'in the manner of obsequies' is well established by Schmidt and Onions, and the line context (Anne performing funeral rites) confirms it unambiguously.

anchor_text: key-cold figure of a holy king
summary: 'Key-cold' is an intensifying compound meaning as cold as a metal key — the proverbial standard for something icy to the touch. Applied to Henry VI's corpse, the phrase stresses that the body has already lost body heat, turning the king's warmth into an image of death's finality.
detail: The compound appears in Lucrece l. 1774 ('And now this pale swan in her watery nest / Begins the sad dirge of her certain ending; ... key-cold') and was a recognized colloquial intensifier. anchor_text: Edward thy son, that now is Prince of Wales, For Edward our son, that was Prince of Wales, Die in his youth by like untimely violence
summary: Margaret constructs her curses as formal symmetrical exchanges, matching each Yorkist possession to a Lancastrian loss. Her son Edward, Prince of Wales — the Lancastrian heir killed at Tewkesbury (1471) — is set against Queen Elizabeth's son Edward, the current Prince of Wales and heir to the throne. The curse is precise: the new Edward should die young by violence, as her Edward did. It is fulfilled when the young Edward V is smothered in the Tower.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the killing of the Lancastrian Edward, Prince of Wales, at Tewkesbury, 4 May 1471.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 639

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) records the killing of the Lancastrian Edward, Prince of Wales, at Tewkesbury (4 May 1471) — the citation is accurate and directly supports the historical background claimed.

The annotation correctly identifies the formal symmetry of Margaret's curse-exchanges (matching Lancastrian loss against Yorkist possession) and the fulfillment of this specific curse when Edward V is killed in the Tower; framing the young princes' fate here is appropriate since the play presents it as prophetic.

anchor_text: Have done thy charm, thou hateful wither'd hag
summary: 'Charm' here means a spoken incantation or spell, not something pleasant — from Latin carmen, a song or verse used in magic. Richard's contemptuous reply casts Margaret's formal cursing not as prayer or prophecy but as witchcraft, dismissing her as a 'hag' (an old witch). The play holds these two possibilities — prophet of God versus pagan witch — in deliberate tension throughout Margaret's role.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'charm' n. 3: 'The chanting or recitation of a verse supposed to possess magic power; an incantation, spell.' From Latin carmen.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 655
OED 'charm' n. 3 ('the chanting or recitation of a verse supposed to possess magic power; an incantation, spell'; from Latin carmen) is a real entry that supports the etymology and sense as claimed.

The etymology of 'charm' from Latin carmen and the reading of Richard's response as casting Margaret's curses as witchcraft while the play maintains ambiguity between prophet and witch is an accurate and defensible mainstream reading.

anchor_text: The worm of conscience still be-gnaw thy soul
summary: The image of a worm gnawing the conscience comes from Isaiah 66:24 ('their worm shall not die'), quoted by Jesus in Mark 9:44 and 9:48 as a description of hell: 'where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.' The 'worm of conscience' became a standard Elizabethan metaphor for the unquiet, guilt-ridden soul. Margaret's curse aims precisely at this: Richard's own guilty conscience as his perpetual tormentor — which is exactly what the ghost-visitation scene (5.3) fulfils.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Mark 9:44 (Geneva 1599): 'Where their worme dieth not, and the fire never goeth out.' Cf. Isaiah 66:24 (Geneva 1599).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 662
Mark 9:44 in the Geneva Bible 1599 reads 'Where their worme dieth not, and the fire never goeth out' — confirmed correct; the Isaiah 66:24 cross-reference is also accurate.

The allusion to Isaiah 66:24 / Mark 9:44/48 ('their worm dieth not') as the source of the 'worm of conscience' motif is standard biblical scholarship; the connection to Richard's guilty dreams in 5.3 is a recognized dramatic fulfillment of this curse.

anchor_text: Thou elvish-mark'd, abortive, rooting hog! Thou that wast seal'd in thy nativity The slave of nature and the son of hell
summary: 'Elvish-mark'd' means bearing marks placed at birth by malevolent fairy spirits — a deformed body taken as a sign of evil nature. 'Abortive' means monstrous or incomplete, born before full term. 'Rooting hog' ties Richard directly to his heraldic badge, the white boar, which roots in the earth — here turned from a symbol of power into one of beastly destruction. 'Seal'd in thy nativity' continues the idea: Richard was stamped with damnation from the moment of birth. This whole curse-stanza is the play's richest cluster of the 'boar' imagery.
detail: Richard's own opening soliloquy (1.1) describes himself as 'deform'd, unfinish'd, sent before my time / Into this breathing world, scarce half made up'; he too uses his deformity as the sign of his nature. Margaret's 'elvish-mark'd' picks up the belief that changelings and deformed children were fairy substitutions. The 'rooting hog' links the heraldic white boar to animal destructiveness — digging up what was planted, destroying what it finds. Tudor sources magnified a real but lesser scoliosis into a full 'crookback.'

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Richard's deformity and the Tudor tradition of reading it as a sign of his character.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'elvish': 'relating to elves, used to express anything mysterious or malicious.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 668

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does describe Richard's deformity and the Tudor tradition of interpreting it as a sign of character; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'elvish' is a real entry supporting the sense claimed.

All three elements — 'elvish-mark'd' as fairy/changeling deformation, 'abortive' as monstrous birth, and 'rooting hog' as the white-boar heraldic badge turned to bestial destruction — are well-grounded in the play's own language and in Elizabethan cultural context; the note about modern archaeology revising Tudor accounts of Richard's scoliosis is appropriately framed as Tudor exaggeration.

anchor_text: Thou rag of honour! thou detested-- Margaret. Richard!
summary: Margaret's tirade is cut off mid-curse when she inadvertently speaks Richard's name. Richard seizes on it to interrupt her and 'complete' the curse himself — substituting his own name for whatever epithet she intended. The joke: by naming him, the curse turns on her (as Elizabeth then notes). It is a piece of stage wit that gives Richard the last word in the most concentrated burst of cursing in the scene. A 'rag of honour' is a shred or remnant of it — all that is left after the cloth of honour has been torn away.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'rag': 'a fragment, a remnant' — contemptuous diminutive.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 673
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'rag' ('a fragment, a remnant' — used contemptuously) is a real entry that supports the sense claimed.

The reading of the interrupted curse as a piece of stage wit in which Richard hijacks Margaret's tirade by supplying his own name is the standard interpretation; 'rag' as shred or remnant is correct, and the note that Elizabeth then points out the curse has turned on Margaret (TLN 683) is accurate to the text.

anchor_text: Poor painted queen, vain flourish of my fortune! Why strew'st thou sugar on that bottled spider, Whose deadly web ensnareth thee about
summary: Margaret calls Queen Elizabeth a 'painted queen' — a mere surface copy of royal dignity, painted rather than genuine (like a stage prop). 'Vain flourish of my fortune' means an empty ornament on what was Margaret's throne. 'Bottled spider' is the most striking image: a spider whose swollen body is like a bottle or gourd — large in the middle, dangerous. Richard will ensnare Elizabeth in his web just as a spider traps a fly. The whole speech has the compressed ferocity of a prophetic warning.
detail: The 'painted queen' image plays on the Elizabethan distrust of cosmetics as concealment of truth (compare the skull beneath paint in Hamlet). 'Bottled' meant bloated or rotund — specifically the body-shape of a bottle spider; Richard is repeatedly described in such animal terms (toad, hog, spider) that flatten his human identity into a predator. The prediction proves accurate: Richard later pretends to woo Elizabeth's daughter through her.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bottled' adj. 2: 'Shaped like a bottle, big-bellied, protuberant' — applied to spiders in several Elizabethan texts.

sources.name: Spivack, Shakespeare and the Allegory of Evil
sources.citation: Spivack, B. (1958). Shakespeare and the Allegory of Evil. Columbia UP, on the animal imagery applied to stage villains.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 684

OED 'bottled' adj. 2 ('shaped like a bottle, big-bellied, protuberant') is a confirmed entry, with the earliest OED evidence from Shakespeare's own usage; Spivack (1958) is a genuine work covering animal imagery for stage villains.

The 'painted queen' as a surface-without-substance image and 'bottled spider' as a bloated predator are both standard readings; the claim that Richard later 'woos Elizabeth's daughter through her' is accurate to Act 4.4.

anchor_text: Peace, master marquis, you are malapert: Your fire-new stamp of honour is scarce current
summary: 'Malapert' means impudent or presumptuous. 'Fire-new stamp of honour' is a coinage metaphor: just as a new coin is freshly stamped ('fire-new,' still hot from the mint), Dorset's rank is so recently acquired that it is 'scarce current' — not yet accepted at face value. Dorset has just told Margaret to be quiet; she turns his youth and new title against him. 'Fire-new' (brand-new) appears several times in Shakespeare for this mockingly fresh quality.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'malapert' adj.: 'Presumptuous, impudent, saucy'; from French mal + apert, open/bold.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'fire-new' adj.: 'Fresh from the fire, brand-new' — applied to coins just minted and to newly-conferred honours.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 698
OED 'malapert' adj. ('presumptuous, impudent') and OED 'fire-new' adj. ('brand-new, fresh from the fire') are both real entries that directly support the senses and etymologies claimed.

Both vocabulary glosses are accurate — 'malapert' as impudent and 'fire-new stamp' as a coinage metaphor for a freshly-conferred honour — and the reading that Margaret turns Dorset's interruption back on him by mocking the recency of his title is sound.

anchor_text: Our aery buildeth in the cedar's top, And dallies with the wind, and scorns the sun
summary: An 'aery' (also 'eyrie') is an eagle's or hawk's nest at a great height. Richard claims his line nests at the summit of the cedar — the tree traditionally symbolic of royal or divinely appointed power — playing with the wind and contemptuous of the sun. It is an image of supreme, fearless elevation. Margaret then takes the same image and turns it: his 'aery' was built in what was her family's nest, and the sun he scorns is her murdered son.
detail: The cedar was associated with Lebanon and with kingly power in the Bible (Ezekiel 17:3-4, 31:3) and in classical poetry. Richard's boast is also self-incriminating: to 'dally with the wind and scorn the sun' evokes the Icarian over-reacher who soars too high. Margaret's counter at line 709-715 — 'thou turn'st the sun to shade' and 'your aery buildeth in our aery's nest' — is a brilliant formal riposte, echoing his own claim word for word to expose the usurpation.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'aery' (eyrie) n.1: 'The nest of an eagle or other bird of prey, placed on a cliff or in a high tree.'

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Ezekiel 17:3 (Geneva 1599): the great eagle that set the 'highest branch of the cedar' — a common royal-power symbol.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 707

OED 'aery' n.1 ('the nest of an eagle or other bird of prey') is confirmed; Geneva Bible 1599 Ezekiel 17:3 does describe a great eagle taking 'the hiest branch of the cedar' as a royal-power symbol — both sources are real and supportive.

The 'aery' as eagle's nest, the cedar as a symbol of royal or divinely appointed power, and Margaret's formal counter-use of Richard's own image (TLN 713: 'Your aery buildeth in our aery's nest') are all accurately described; the Icarian over-reacher parallel is a legitimate secondary resonance, not an overreach.

anchor_text: O princely Buckingham, I'll kiss thy hand, In sign of league and amity with thee
summary: Margaret singles out Buckingham as the one great lord whose hands are not yet stained with her blood, blesses him, and warns him specifically that Richard will destroy him. Her warning — 'When he shall split thy very heart with sorrow, / And say, poor Margaret was a prophetess!' — is the play's most pointed prophecy. Buckingham is Richard's closest ally in the first half of the play and is executed by his order in Act 5. When Buckingham goes to his death, he will remember this scene.
detail: Henry Stafford, Duke of Buckingham, was historically Richard's chief instrument in the usurpation — coaching the citizens, managing the intimidation of the council, and engineering Richard's acceptance of the crown. When he later asked for the earldom of Hereford that Richard had promised, Richard refused; Buckingham raised a rebellion that collapsed and he was captured and beheaded at Salisbury on 2 November 1483. More's History reports his execution; Shakespeare stages it in 5.1 with Buckingham himself recalling Margaret's prophecy.

sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (written c. 1513-18; printed 1557), on Buckingham's role in the usurpation and his execution, 1483.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Duke of Buckingham's rebellion and execution.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 723

More's History of Richard III covers Buckingham's role in the usurpation and his execution at Salisbury (2 November 1483); Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) also records the rebellion and execution — both citations are accurate.

The annotation accurately summarizes Margaret's blessing-and-warning to Buckingham, the historical facts of his role in the usurpation and his execution in November 1483, and the dramatic fulfillment in 5.1 where Buckingham recalls the prophecy.

anchor_text: I cannot blame her: by God's holy mother, She hath had too much wrong; and I repent My part thereof
summary: Richard publicly offers a performance of remorse once Margaret has left, swearing 'by God's holy mother' — a Catholic oath by the Virgin Mary — and expressing apparent guilt for his wrongs to Margaret. The audience knows from the soliloquy that follows (lines 767-781) that this is pure hypocrisy: Richard 'do[es] the wrong, and first begin[s] to brawl.' The oath is dramatically ironic: a man who has just planned his brother's murder invoking the mother of God as his witness.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Richard's public persona of piety and private ruthlessness — a character trait emphasised throughout More's and Holinshed's accounts.

sources.name: Spivack, Shakespeare and the Allegory of Evil
sources.citation: Spivack, B. (1958). Shakespeare and the Allegory of Evil. Columbia UP, on the Vice's technique of false piety as cover for villainy.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 749

Holinshed does emphasise Richard's public persona of piety contrasted with private ruthlessness, and Spivack (1958) is a genuine work that analyses the Vice's technique of false piety — both sources support the claim.

The reading of Richard's public remorse as deliberate hypocrisy is unambiguously confirmed by his following soliloquy (TLN 767-781); calling the Marian oath a 'Catholic' oath is accurate for the pre-Reformation register of the oath even in a Protestant theatrical context.

anchor_text: He is frank'd up to fatting for his pains
summary: 'Frank'd up' means shut in a sty to fatten — a 'frank' (or 'franc') was a pen where pigs were enclosed and fattened for slaughter. Richard says Clarence is being 'fattened' in prison — the metaphor makes him livestock being prepared to be killed. It is a casual, horrible image for the murder he has already set in motion, delivered with Richard's characteristic dark wit.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'frank' n.3 and v.3: 'An enclosure for fattening pigs; to shut up in a frank for fattening.' Common figurative use for imprisonment.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'frank': 'to fatten, to pen up for fattening.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 757
OED 'frank' n.3 / v.3 ('an enclosure for fattening pigs; to shut up for fattening') and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'frank' both confirm the sense and figurative use claimed.

The 'frank' as a pig-fattening pen and 'frank'd up to fatting' as imprisonment-before-slaughter is correct; the reading of the metaphor as Richard's casual dark wit — treating Clarence as livestock he has already condemned — is fully warranted.

anchor_text: with a piece of Scripture, Tell them that God bids us do good for evil: And thus I clothe my naked villany With odd old ends stol'n forth of holy writ; And seem a saint when most I play the devil
summary: Richard confesses in soliloquy that he weaponises Scripture, citing the Christian teaching that one should 'do good for evil' — drawn from Matthew 5:44 ('do good to them that hate you') or Romans 12:21 ('overcome evil with good') — not because he believes it but as rhetorical armour. He 'clothes' his villainy in 'holy writ' to 'seem a saint when most I play the devil.' The speech is the play's clearest statement of Richard as a hypocritical stage Machiavel who uses religion as camouflage.
detail: More's History of Richard III stresses Richard's use of pious displays — two bishops carried before him when he appeared before the citizens, a prayer book ostentatiously in hand — as techniques of performance. Richard's phrase 'odd old ends stol'n forth of holy writ' is deliberately irreverent: Scripture is a wardrobe from which he steals scraps as disguise. The Vice of the morality plays similarly quoted Scripture to tempt the hero.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Romans 12:21 (Geneva 1599): 'Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with goodness.' Matthew 5:44 (Geneva 1599): 'Love your enemies; bless them that curse you; do good to them that hate you.'

sources.name: More, History of Richard III
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (written c. 1513-18; printed 1557), on Richard's studied displays of religious piety as political performance.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 777

Geneva Bible 1599 Romans 12:21 ('Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with goodness') and Matthew 5:44 are confirmed accurate; More's History of Richard III does specifically describe Richard's staged piety with bishops and prayer book.

The identification of 'do good for evil' with Romans 12:21 and Matthew 5:44 is accurate; the Vice-parallel (quoting scripture to tempt) and More's emphasis on Richard's ostentatious piety as political performance are mainstream observations that the annotation represents honestly.

anchor_text: repair to Crosby Place
summary: Crosby Place (later Crosby Hall) was a large late-medieval mansion in Bishopsgate, London, built in the 1460s and leased by Richard, Duke of Gloucester, from about 1483. He used it as his London base during the period of the usurpation. Shakespeare's reference is accurate: More's History of Richard III mentions Crosby Place as Richard's headquarters. Part of the original great hall survives and was relocated to Chelsea in the early twentieth century.

sources.name: More, History of Richard III
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (written c. 1513-18; printed 1557), on Crosby Place as Richard's London residence.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 788
More's History of Richard III does mention Crosby Place as Richard's London base, and the historical record confirms Richard leased Crosby Place in Bishopsgate — the citation is accurate.

Crosby Place as Richard's London base is historically accurate and supported by More; the note about the great hall being relocated to Chelsea in the early twentieth century is a factual aside that is correct.

anchor_text: Your eyes drop millstones when fools' eyes fall tears
summary: Richard praises the murderers for their hardness: where a fool's eyes 'fall tears,' theirs 'drop millstones' — heavy grindstones incapable of weeping. The antithesis flatters them as tougher than ordinary men. The image of weeping millstones (impossibly hard objects substituted for soft tears) is an ironic hyperbole that also mocks the very idea of compassion. The line is Richard at his most coldly witty, bonding with hired killers by celebrating their incapacity for feeling.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'millstone': proverbially used from the 16th century in the phrase 'to weep millstones' for the hardest possible heart, unable to weep real tears — the direct opposite of 'eye-drops' or tears.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 796
OED 'millstone' records the proverbial use ('to weep millstones') as a 16th-century idiom for extreme hardness of heart — the source supports the claim.

The antithesis of millstones versus tears as a hyperbolic compliment to the murderers' hard-heartedness is the obvious reading; 'weep millstones' as a proverbial Elizabethan phrase for a heart incapable of weeping is well-attested.

anchor_text: pass'd a miserable night, So full of fearful dreams
summary: Clarence's opening speech establishes the scene's central action: a man telling the dream that foreshadows his own death. In Renaissance psychology dreams were believed to carry genuine prophetic weight, produced either by God, the devil, or the humors — Clarence's terror is not mere superstition but a serious premonition.
detail: The tradition of prophetic death-dreams runs through medieval and early-modern literature from Chaucer's Troilus to the Mirror for Magistrates. Shakespeare makes Clarence's dream far more elaborate than the bare chronicle entry — Holinshed records the death but not the dream. The elaborateness signals that the audience should read this as prophetically serious, not atmospheric padding: the dream predicts the exact manner of death (drowning) that closes the scene.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on the death of Clarence.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 801
Holinshed 1587 does record the death of Clarence without an elaborate dream; the claim that Shakespeare elaborates beyond the chronicle is accurate and the citation is real and supportive.

The claim that Renaissance audiences took prophetic dreams seriously as genuine premonitions (not mere atmosphere) is mainstream, and the annotation correctly notes that Shakespeare's elaboration beyond Holinshed signals intentional prophetic weight culminating in the malmsey drowning.

anchor_text: broken from the Tower, And was embark'd to cross to Burgundy
summary: Clarence dreams of escaping the Tower of London and sailing for Burgundy, the duchy in what is now Belgium and the Netherlands. Burgundy was a natural refuge for Yorkists: Edward IV had sheltered there during his exile in 1470-71, and Clarence himself had briefly allied with the Burgundian court during the wars.
detail: The Tower of London served throughout the Middle Ages as a royal prison for political detainees; by Shakespeare's audience it was intimately associated with judicial murders, including those of Henry VI and the young princes. Burgundy's importance in the York/Lancaster struggle is noted throughout the Henry VI plays — its duke shifted allegiance from the English to the French during the Hundred Years' War, but the Yorkist connection endured through Edward IV's period of exile. Clarence's dream-geography thus has plausible historical logic.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Edward IV's exile in Burgundy, 1470-71, and Clarence's political career.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 808
Holinshed 1587 records Edward IV's exile in Burgundy (1470-71) and Clarence's changing allegiances; the citation is real and directly supports the claim.

The Burgundy reference is historically grounded — Edward IV's 1470-71 exile there is well-documented, and Clarence's Yorkist connections to Burgundy give the dream-geography plausible historical logic without over-reading.

anchor_text: cited up a thousand heavy times, During the wars of York and Lancaster
summary: 'Cited up' means called to mind, recalled. Clarence and Gloucester, standing on the ship's deck looking back toward England, remember all the disasters they lived through during the Wars of the Roses — the dynastic civil wars between the houses of York and Lancaster that consumed their entire adult lives.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cite' v. 5: 'to call to mind, recite.'

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Wars of the Roses.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 813
OED s.v. 'cite' v. 5 ('to call to mind') and Holinshed on the Wars of the Roses are both real and supportive of the archaic-vocabulary and historical claims.
'Cited up' as 'called to mind / recalled' is defensible from OED usage, and the gloss that they are remembering wartime disasters while looking back toward England matches TLN 812-815 exactly.

anchor_text: Inestimable stones, unvalued jewels, All scatt'red in the bottom of the sea
summary: 'Inestimable' means too precious to be priced; 'unvalued' here means beyond valuation (priceless), not worthless — a common Elizabethan sense. The dream-inventory of treasure lying among bones is a formal rhetorical device called enargeia (vivid description that makes the listener see the scene), but it also functions as a memento mori: all earthly wealth lies useless at the bottom of the sea, winking from dead men's skulls.
detail: The image of scattered treasure among the dead at the seabed descends from a long tradition of seabed-as-charnel-house imagery. It anticipates the scene's final action: Clarence himself will be 'drowned' in the malmsey-butt and become, in a sense, a body among riches (the nobleman reduced to a tavern barrel). The 'reflecting gems' in empty eye-sockets is among Shakespeare's most vivid images of death's mockery of vanity.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'unvalued' adj. 1: 'inestimable, priceless' (citing this passage).

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'inestimable': 'that cannot be valued, invaluable.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 826
OED 'unvalued' adj. 1 ('inestimable, priceless') is a well-attested sense citing this very passage, and Schmidt s.v. 'inestimable' is standard; both citations are real and supportive.

'Unvalued' as 'priceless / beyond valuation' is the correct Elizabethan sense here (not 'worthless'), and the memento mori / enargeia reading is mainstream; the note that the seabed image anticipates Clarence becoming a body among riches is an interpretive extension but defensible given the scene's resolution.

anchor_text: yield the ghost: but still the envious flood Stopp'd in my soul
summary: 'Yield the ghost' means to give up the soul — to die. 'Ghost' here is the older sense of the soul or life-breath (Old English gast), not a haunting spirit. The flood is 'envious' in the sense of hostile, malicious; it grudges Clarence the release of death. The soul, unable to escape through the lungs, is smothered 'within my panting bulk' — his heaving body.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ghost' n. I.1: 'the soul or spirit, as the principle of life'; s.v. 'yield' v. 28: 'yield up the ghost, to die.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'envious' adj. 3: 'malicious, malignant, hurtful.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 836

OED s.v. 'ghost' n. I.1 ('soul or spirit') and s.v. 'yield' v. 28 ('yield up the ghost, to die'), and OED 'envious' adj. 3 ('malicious, malignant') are all genuine entries that support the archaic-vocabulary claims.

'Ghost' as soul/life-breath (OE gast) and 'envious' as malicious are both standard Elizabethan usages well supported by OED, and the reading that the flood grudges Clarence the release of death fits the lines exactly.

anchor_text: pass'd, methought, the melancholy flood With that grim ferryman which poets write of
summary: The 'melancholy flood' is the river Styx (or Acheron) of classical mythology — the river of the underworld that the dead must cross to reach their final home. The 'grim ferryman' is Charon, who transported souls across it for a coin. Clarence has not merely drowned in his dream: he has passed into the classical afterlife.
detail: The phrase 'which poets write of' is Clarence's own editorial note — he knows this is the stuff of ancient poetry, not Christian theology. Yet in the same speech he will describe the encounter with the shades of Warwick and Prince Edward in language that blends classical Hades with a Christian hell ('legion of foul fiends,' 'Furies'). Shakespeare deliberately fuses the two afterlife traditions, giving Clarence's conscience a double frame: classical guilt (perjury and betrayal) and Christian damnation. Virgil's description of Charon ferrying the dead across the underworld river (Aeneid 6) was the standard classical reference, well known to educated Elizabethans through grammar-school Latin.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 6.298-316 (Charon and the crossing of the river of the dead).

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4 (Juno's descent to the underworld) and 10 (Orpheus): the Styx and the realm of the dead as Shakespeare's educated audience knew them through Golding's 1567 English Ovid.

anchor_text: my great father-in-law, renowned Warwick; Who spake aloud, What scourge for perjury
summary: Clarence's 'great father-in-law' is Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, known as 'the Kingmaker' — the most powerful magnate of the Wars of the Roses. Warwick's daughter Isabel had married Clarence; Warwick himself died at the Battle of Barnet (1471) after Clarence defected from the Lancastrian cause they had joined together, returning to his brother Edward IV. Warwick's ghost accuses Clarence of 'perjury' — breaking his sworn oath to the Lancastrian cause.
detail: Warwick had engineered the brief restoration of Henry VI in 1470; Clarence had followed him but then switched sides back to Edward IV before Barnet, a betrayal that contributed directly to Warwick's defeat and death. The accusation 'false Clarence' in the next lines pinpoints this as the perjury at issue. Holinshed and Hall recount the political gymnastics of Clarence's allegiance-changes in detail; More's History stresses the treachery.

anchor_text: A shadow like an Angel, with bright hair Dabbled in blood; and he shriek'd out aloud Clarence is come,--false, fleeting, perjur'd Clarence,-- That stabb'd me in the field by Tewksbury

The prince accuses Clarence of betraying the very cause he had sworn to uphold when he joined Warwick. 'Fleeting' here means inconstant, changeable — a man who fled from one loyalty to another.
detail: The historical killing of Prince Edward at Tewkesbury (4 May 1471) was brutal and contested. Holinshed says he was cut down fleeing the field; More and later Tudor sources say he was taken prisoner and then stabbed by Edward IV, Clarence, and Richard of Gloucester in cold blood after the battle. Shakespeare uses this second, darker tradition. The phrase 'false, fleeting, perjur'd Clarence' is one of the play's great rhetorical triads: three adjectives summarizing his entire political career. The accusation also links back to the play's opening — Richard in 1.1 has already engineered Clarence's imprisonment on the letter 'G' prophecy, part of his systematic removal of rivals.

summary: The Furies (Greek Erinyes, Latin Furiae) were the female spirits of divine vengeance in classical mythology, who tormented those guilty of the worst crimes — especially murder of kin and perjury. They are the appropriate tormentors for Clarence, who has both sworn a perjured oath and betrayed a father-in-law (a kin-bond). The Prince's cry fuses classical and Christian punishment: 'a legion of foul fiends' in the next line is the New Testament demonic language.

anchor_text: For Edward's sake; and see how he requites me
summary: 'He requites me' — he repays me (with imprisonment). Clarence tells Brakenbury that his evil deeds were done for his brother Edward IV's sake, yet Edward is now the one who has locked him in the Tower. The dramatic irony is sharp: Clarence believes Edward imprisoned him on misguided advice and does not suspect that Richard engineered his downfall. 'Requite' means to repay, especially a past service or injury — here bitterly: Clarence served his brother with crimes and is repaid with a prison cell.

anchor_text: Sorrow breaks seasons and reposing hours, Makes the night morning and the noontide night
summary: Brakenbury's four-line soliloquy is a formal sententious commentary on the scene (a 'sententia' — a moralizing maxim used in classical rhetoric and Elizabethan drama to close or frame a scene). 'Breaks seasons' means disrupts the natural order of time. The couplet form and balanced antithesis ('night morning... noontide night') mark it as a set-piece gnome — a general truth extracted from a particular case — and give Brakenbury an unexpected moment of moral gravity before he hands Clarence over to his killers.

anchor_text: he shall never wake until the great judgment-day
summary: The 'great judgment day' is the Last Judgment of Christian theology — the day at the end of time when God will raise all the dead and judge them for their lives. summary: The Second Murderer distinguishes between earthly and divine authority: a royal warrant ('commission') can authorize killing in the eyes of the law, but no written document can exempt a man from God's judgment. anchor_text: my holy humour will change; it was wont to hold me but while one tells twenty
summary: 'Humour' here means a mood or passing fit (from the older medical theory that four bodily humors governed temperament). anchor_text: there's few or none will entertain it
summary: The Second Murderer's extended comic monologue on conscience is the scene's philosophical centerpiece. 'Entertain' means to welcome as a guest, to keep in one's service (a retained servant was 'entertained'). He is running through the things conscience prevents — theft, lying, adultery — and concluding that no one will 'keep' conscience in employment. The joke is that he speaks about conscience as if it were a troublesome lodger or servant to be turned out: 'it is turned out of towns and cities for a dangerous thing.'

The murderer's comedy and Clarence's theology answer each other: both are about the same law, but the murderer treats it as a social inconvenience and Clarence treats it as divine sanction. 'Entertain' in the sense of 'to retain a servant' is the key meaning here; conscience is being fired.

anchor_text: Take him on the costard with the hilts of thy sword, and then throw him in the malmsey-butt
summary: A 'costard' is the head (literally a large kind of apple, used colloquially for the head). 'Hilts' means the handle of the sword — the plan is to knock Clarence unconscious with the pommel, not to stab him. A 'malmsey-butt' is a large cask (a 'butt' = about 108 gallons) of malmsey, a sweet Mediterranean wine. The historical tradition, recorded in Holinshed and More, is that Clarence was drowned in a barrel of malmsey — the play stages that notoriety.

The method of execution is comically undignified for a duke — wine-barrel drowning — which is precisely the point: Clarence has been devalued to a body to be disposed of in any convenient receptacle. Holinshed records the malmsey-butt tradition as fact; modern historians regard it as possibly legendary but widely believed in Shakespeare's time.

summary: A 'sop' is bread or food dipped and soaked in wine — a common table practice. The Second Murderer proposes to make Clarence literally a sop by drowning him in the malmsey cask. A 'sop' was also a gift or bribe ('a sop to Cerberus' — giving the hellhound food to quiet him), and in that sense there may be a secondary jest: Clarence, having been a treacherous schemer who took bribes and switched sides, becomes himself the 'sop.' anchor_text: Erroneous vassals! the great King of kings Hath in the table of his law commanded That thou shalt do no murder
summary: 'The great King of kings' is a biblical title for God — used repeatedly in Revelation and in the Old Testament to distinguish God from earthly monarchs. 'The table of his law' refers to the Ten Commandments, originally written by God on stone tablets (the two 'tables' given to Moses on Sinai). Clarence is invoking the Sixth Commandment: 'Thou shalt not kill' (Exodus 20:13). He is arguing that the murderers' obedience to an earthly king cannot override God's direct command.

anchor_text: Thou didst receive the sacrament to fight In quarrel of the house of Lancaster
summary: Receiving the sacrament — the Eucharist (Holy Communion) — while swearing an oath was the most solemn form of pledge available; breaking it was a mortal sin. The Second Murderer is pointing out that when Clarence joined the Earl of Warwick's Lancastrian rebellion in 1470, he sealed that alliance with a sworn sacramental oath. His defection back to Edward IV before Barnet was therefore not merely political betrayal but sacrilege.
detail: The murderers' counterargument is legally and theologically sharp: Clarence has invoked God's law against murder, but God's law also forbids perjury — and Clarence broke a sacred oath. He cannot call God as his protector when he himself sinned against God's law by forswearing a sacramental vow. This exchange raises the play's central irony: Clarence's genuine guilt (perjury, complicity in the killing of Prince Edward) does not make his murder just, but it does strip him of the moral authority to command God's protection on the basis of his innocence alone.

Taking the sacrament to swear an oath was indeed the most solemn pledge in early-modern practice, and Clarence's historical defection from the Lancastrian cause after sealing it with such an oath is accurately described; the murderers' counter-argument (perjury also violates God's law) is correctly identified as the theologically sharp reply it is.

anchor_text: Take not the quarrel from His powerful arm; He needs no indirect or lawless course To cut off those that have offended Him
summary: Clarence argues that God does not need human agents working through unlawful means to punish sinners: God avenges directly when He wills. The argument is drawn from the biblical principle that vengeance belongs to God alone. 'Take not the quarrel from his powerful arm' means: do not seize God's prerogative of punishment for yourselves.

Clarence's argument is theologically sound but practically desperate: he is trying to keep two hired killers from murdering him. The irony is layered — the same argument that forbids them to kill him also forbids the revenge he himself took at Tewkesbury.

anchor_text: If you are hir'd for meed, go back again, And I will send you to my brother Gloster, Who shall reward you better for my life
summary: 'Meed' means reward, payment, wages — often specifically a mercenary fee. Clarence is offering to outbid Richard: if the murderers are working for money rather than loyalty, he will pay them more to let him live and carry a message to Gloucester (still believing, fatally, that Richard is his ally). summary: After helping murder Clarence, the Second Murderer compares himself to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor who washed his hands before the crowd when he handed Jesus over to be crucified — a gesture meant to declare himself innocent of blood he was about to spill. The Second Murderer's conscience, which kept breaking through the scene, finally wins: he refuses the reward and exits, leaving his partner to finish the disposal alone.

anchor_text: A pleasing cordial, princely Buckingham

detail: In Elizabethan medicine, cordials were warm, sweet preparations — often of spiced wine or herbal distillations — given to revive failing patients, especially those with weak hearts. The word pairs with 'sickly heart' (TLN 1113) to insist on Edward's physical decline even as he exercises royal authority. The metaphor of political reconciliation as medical remedy runs through the scene: the king's body politic can only be healed if his feuding court makes peace around his body natural.

The audience watching knows Richard has already ended Clarence's 'period' by having him drowned.

anchor_text: Among this princely heap, if any here, By false intelligence or wrong surmise, Hold me a foe
summary: Richard's speech of self-exculpation (TLN 1123-1144) is a masterpiece of performed innocence: he invites anyone with a grudge to speak, attributes every possible enmity to others' 'false intelligence' (misinformation) rather than his own actions, and ends with the line 'I thank my God for my humility.' To a knowing audience, every word is a lie — he has just had his brother Clarence murdered.
detail: The rhetorical form is paradiastole: the relabeling of a vice as a virtue. Richard first lists every possible grievance as a misunderstanding ('if I unwittingly, or in my rage, / Have aught committed that is hardly borne'), then closes by thanking God for a virtue — humility — that no other character in the play would grant him. The speech echoes the confessional language of penitence; in context it is the Vice figure's most polished mask. Thomas More's History of Richard III (c. 1513-18, via Holinshed 1587) paints Richard as the supreme dissembler whose 'countenance was dissembling' even as he planned murder.

Labelling Richard's speech 'paradiastole' is a stretch — paradiastole relabels a vice as a virtue within a single utterance, whereas Richard's speech is a protracted profession of innocence; the Vice-figure frame and the dramatic-irony reading are sound, but the specific rhetorical label is imprecise enough to warrant caution.

anchor_text: I thank my God for my humility
summary: The line is a studied climax of dramatic irony: Richard is the least humble character in the play — he has just had his own brother drowned — and he crowns a speech of fraudulent innocence by thanking God for a virtue no one in the audience believes he possesses.
detail: Richard uses a formulaic Protestant piety ('I thank my God') as a prop in his theatrical performance of virtue, capping the self-exculpation speech with what amounts to a joke that only the audience can appreciate. The same technique — pious language in the mouth of a murderer — runs through his later manipulation of the citizens and the Lord Mayor in 3.7. Richard's aside to himself when Queen Elizabeth asks for Clarence is therefore the moment the mask slips for the court: he has let the death go further than needed.

sources.name: More / Holinshed

anchor_text: a winged Mercury did bear; Some tardy cripple bore the countermand That came too lag
summary: Mercury (Greek Hermes) was the winged messenger-god of classical mythology, the fastest of the Olympians. Richard sardonically contrasts him with a 'tardy cripple': the fast order to kill Clarence was executed in full, while the 'countermand' (revocation) arrived too slowly to stop it. The contrast is grotesque wit — and a lie, since Richard ensured the countermand came too late.
detail: Mercury's winged sandals (talaria) and helmet (petasus) were stock emblems of speed in classical and Renaissance iconography; Ovid describes him at Metamorphoses 1.671-672. 'Lag' means 'late, too far behind' (OED s.v. 'lag,' adj., sense 1), surviving in modern English as 'lagging.' Richard's framing is calculated: he implies the execution was the king's order faithfully and swiftly carried out, the countermand the court's failure to move quickly enough. The entire explanation redistributes guilt from Richard to the dead king and the watching lords — a characteristic Machiavellian maneuver.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.671-672 (Mercury, talaria-shod, the swift messenger of the gods).

Mercury as the winged messenger-god, contrasted with a 'tardy cripple,' is a standard classical allusion and Richard's Machiavellian redistribution of guilt to the king and court is unambiguously what the speech does; the reading does not overreach.

anchor_text: Have I a tongue to doom my brother's death, And shall that tongue give pardon to a slave? My brother kill'd no man,--his fault was thought
summary: Edward's speech (TLN 1174-1204) is a long anaphora — a list of parallel questions all beginning 'Who...?' — that tears apart his own guilt for Clarence's death. The key contrast here is between Clarence, who 'kill'd no man' but was executed for thought-crime (the prophecy about 'G'), and a common servant who committed actual murder and may receive pardon.
detail: The anaphora ('Who told me... Who told me... Who spoke of...') is the rhetorical form of the penitential lament — the king indicting himself before God and his court. The distinction between punishing 'thought' and pardoning 'deed' was legally sharp in Tudor England: actual treason required an overt act; punishing mere intent was associated with tyranny and with Henry VIII's use of the treason laws. Historically, Clarence was attainted by Act of Parliament (February 1478) and the charges included treasonous 'imaginations' and a claim to the succession, as well as accusations of spreading rumours about Edward's bastardy; the parliamentary attainder made execution legal but not necessarily just.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): the attainder and private execution of George, Duke of Clarence, 1478, at the Tower of London; his fault was 'imagining' the king's death, not an overt act.

sources.name: More / Holinshed

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1174

The anaphoric structure of Edward's lament is correctly identified, the contrast between punishing thought-crime and pardoning actual murder is textually explicit, and the historical note about Clarence's attainder being based on 'imaginations' rather than overt acts is accurate.

anchor_text: your carters or your waiting-vassals Have done a drunken slaughter, and defac'd The precious image of our dear Redeemer
summary: 'Carters' are cart-drivers; 'waiting-vassals' are household servants. Edward's point is that the great lords intercede with the king for the crimes of their lowliest servants, but no one interceded for his royal brother. 'The precious image of our dear Redeemer' alludes to Genesis 1:27: humankind is made in God's image, so to kill any person is to destroy God's image — a stronger claim for Clarence, who was also a prince and God's anointed by blood.
detail: The doctrine that every human being bears the imago Dei (image of God) — derived from Genesis 1:27 ('So God created man in his owne image,' Geneva 1599) — was a commonplace of Protestant preaching and gave murder a theological weight beyond civil crime. Edward draws on it to argue that a drunk servant killing in a brawl is a smaller offense against the divine image than the calculated murder of a royal prince-brother. Theologically, the argument also anticipates the Sixth Commandment frame (Exodus 20:13), linking Clarence's death to fratricide and the Cain-and-Abel archetype.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Genesis 1:27 (Geneva 1599): 'So God created man in his owne image: in the image of God created he him.' The doctrine that murder defaced the imago Dei was a standard Elizabethan homiletic argument.

The imago Dei allusion via Genesis 1:27 and 9:6 is the mainstream reading of 'precious image of our dear Redeemer' — Elizabethan homiletic tradition regularly used both texts to give murder theological weight — and the comparison of servants' crimes with the murder of a royal prince is exactly what the speech argues.

anchor_text: O God, I fear Thy justice will take hold On me, and you, and mine, and yours, for this
summary: Edward's dying fear — that God's justice will punish him, his family ('mine'), and the court ('you and yours') for Clarence's death — is the play's thesis statement for the Tudor providential view of history: sins against kin and against the divine order invite a retribution that falls on descendants as well as on the sinner. This is exactly what the play then dramatizes in Acts 3-5.
detail: The Tudor chroniclers Edward Hall and Raphael Holinshed read the Wars of the Roses as a providential cycle of sin and punishment, with each killing generating the next. Edward's prophecy is both penitential and dramatically prophetic: 'mine' (his children, the princes in the Tower) will be killed by 'yours' (specifically by Richard, Edward's own brother, now standing in the room). Shakespeare makes the dying king a prophet against himself. The same providential logic governs Queen Margaret's curse-speeches, the appearance of the Ghosts at Bosworth, and Richmond's closing prayer.

sources.name: Hall
sources.citation: Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548): the providential reading of the civil wars as divine punishment transmitted into Shakespeare's structural design.

sources.name: Holinshed

anchor_text: This is the fruit of rashness! Mark'd you not How that the guilty kindred of the queen Look'd pale

It is the Machiavel at his most economical: in four lines he converts his own crime into an accusation against his next targets, Rivers, Dorset, and Grey.

The aside-then-exeunt structure is the Vice's signature: Richard first confides the truth to the audience in public, then leads the remaining lords offstage with a performance of concerned loyalty — 'Come, lords, will you go / To comfort Edward with our company?' — exactly paralleling his opening soliloquy's promise to 'prove a villain' while smiling.

anchor_text: My pretty cousins, you mistake me both
summary: 'Cousins' here does not mean children of aunts or uncles. In Tudor usage, any close relative of the same generation or one below — grandchildren included — could be addressed as 'cousin.' The Duchess of York uses it for her dead son Clarence's children, who are her grandchildren.
