The OED documents the usage as common in formal address throughout the sixteenth century; royal and noble households used it between any kin who shared a great-grandparent. The Duchess's affectionate diminutive 'pretty' signals she is addressing children, clarifying the relationship to an audience who might be misled by the word.

anchor_text: my good uncle Gloster Told me, the king, provok'd to it by the queen
summary: Clarence's son believes Richard's lie that the queen, Elizabeth Woodville, manipulated Edward IV into imprisoning their father. Richard has already planted this false account to deflect blame from himself — he personally arranged Clarence's arrest and death — and the child repeats it innocently. This moment shows how thoroughly Richard has manipulated his own family.
detail: The historical sources (More, Holinshed) record that it was Richard and the Buckingham faction who engineered Clarence's execution — the charge of treasonable prophecy was a pretext. Shakespeare dramatizes the irony here with particular cruelty: the murdered man's son unwittingly defends his murderer. The feud between the Woodvilles (Queen Elizabeth's family) and the older Yorkist nobility was real and bitter, making the lie plausible: Clarence had opposed the Woodville marriage and later allied with the Earl of Warwick against Edward IV. Richard exploits this existing animus to construct a false scapegoat. More's History and Holinshed both note Richard's skill at winning the trust of those he intended to destroy.

The scene text confirms the child repeats Richard's lie verbatim (he 'told me... provok'd to it by the queen'), and the historical gloss on the Woodville-Yorkist feud making the lie plausible is mainstream scholarship.

anchor_text: deceit should steal such gentle shape, And with a virtuous visard hide deep vice
summary: A 'visard' (also spelled visor or vizard) is a mask — either the hinged face-guard of a helmet or a stage mask worn to conceal identity. The Duchess of York grieves that Richard's decent outward appearance (his 'gentle shape') serves as a mask hiding his inner wickedness.
detail: The word comes from Old French visiere, from vis (face). By Shakespeare's time 'visard' and 'visor' were interchangeable, both meaning a face-mask worn at masquerades, tournaments, or on stage. The theatrical resonance is pointed: Richard is described throughout the play in terms of acting and disguise, and here his own mother casts him as a performer hiding his true face behind a prop. The contrast between 'virtuous visard' and 'deep vice' also echoes the Vice figure of the morality plays — the character who wore a smiling mask while tempting the hero toward damnation.

anchor_text: from my dugs he drew not this deceit
summary: 'Dugs' means a woman's breasts as milk-giving organs — used here for the act of nursing an infant. The Duchess declares that she did not pass her son Richard's capacity for deceit through her breast milk; the vice is his alone, not inherited from her.

The belief that a mother's character and qualities could be literally transmitted through nursing was a Renaissance medical commonplace, found in sources from Galen through Montaigne; wet-nurses were therefore chosen carefully. The Duchess's disclaimer — 'I did not nurse this evil into him' — is also an expression of shame and disavowal: she can acknowledge him as her son while denying any share in his moral character.

anchor_text: What means this scene of rude impatience? To make an act of tragic violence
summary: The Duchess asks what Queen Elizabeth's wild entrance 'means.' Elizabeth answers in the same theatrical register: she will make 'an act of tragic violence.' 'Scene' and 'act' both carry theatrical meanings (a division of a play, a performance), so the exchange casts grief itself as drama — and prepares the audience to hear the wailing contest that follows as a formal, stylized performance.
detail: Throughout Richard III grief is both deeply felt and stylized into ritualized exchanges — the stichomythic (line-by-line) lament at TLN 1284-1292, the competitive elegies the Duchess pronounces. By introducing the word 'scene' and answering with 'act,' the text frames this mourning as theater within theater — a move consistent with the play's pervasive self-consciousness about acting. Richard is not present in these lines, but the theatrical vocabulary ironically echoes his own language of performance: he called himself 'a player' in the preceding acts. Elizabeth's phrase 'act of tragic violence' also literally describes what is happening: the death of a king is the defining event of tragedy as a genre.

The theatrical double-meaning of 'scene' and 'act' in these two consecutive lines is textually unambiguous, and the reading that it frames stylised grief as theatre-within-theatre is a defensible and mainstream interpretation.

anchor_text: Why grow the branches when the root is gone? Why wither not the leaves that want their sap
summary: Queen Elizabeth figures her dead husband Edward IV as the root and trunk of a tree, and herself and her children as the branches and leaves that cannot survive now that the source of life is cut off. The image was a standard Elizabethan figure for a royal family, where the king is the living root of all his dependants.
detail: The plant-metaphor for royal lineage runs through the history plays: the same cluster of images (roots, branches, grafts, wither, sap) appears in Richard II 2.1, where John of Gaunt mourns England as a 'garden' and in 3 Henry VI where York's genealogical claim is figured as a growing tree. Elizabeth's rhetorical questions — two parallel 'why' clauses — are an example of anaphora (beginning successive clauses with the same word) combined with a pathetic fallacy: nature itself should mourn the dead king. The questions are not really questions but a way of expressing the incomprehensibility of continued life after such a loss — a figure called aporesis (feigned helplessness).

The tree metaphor for royal lineage is accurate and the rhetorical identification of anaphora is correct; the label 'aporesis' for the rhetorical questions overstates precision slightly but is not wrong.

anchor_text: two mirrors of his princely semblance Are crack'd in pieces by malignant death, And I for comfort have but one false glass
summary: The Duchess of York calls Edward IV's two dead sons — Edward IV himself and Clarence — her 'mirrors': as a parent lives on in children who resemble the parent, she had 'looked at' her dead husband in the faces of her surviving sons. Now both are gone. Her one remaining son, the 'false glass,' is Richard — whose image gives her back only her shame, not her husband's likeness.
detail: The conceit of children as mirrors of their parents was a Renaissance literary and theological commonplace, drawn in part from the Sonnets tradition (compare Shakespeare's own Sonnets 1-17, where procreation is urged so the beloved's image is preserved in a child, 'where your sweet semblance to some other give'). Here the image is inverted and darkened: rather than offering comfort, the surviving 'mirror' (Richard) distorts the reflection. 'Semblance' means likeness or image. The Duchess's private acknowledgment that Richard is 'false' — deceptive, wrongly reflecting — is a moment of bitter self-knowledge: she raised the man who will destroy what remains of her family.

sources.name: Schmidt

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1264

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'semblance' is a real reference work that defines the term as 'likeness, image, resemblance'; the children-as-mirrors conceit is a Renaissance commonplace well supported by this lexicographic citation.

The 'mirrors' conceit is clearly supported by the text ('I have bewept a worthy husband's death, And liv'd by looking on his images'), and identifying the 'false glass' with Richard is explicit at TLN 1267 ('That grieves me when I see my shame in him').

anchor_text: Thine being but a moiety of my moan, To overgo thy woes and drown thy cries
summary: A 'moiety' is a half, or more loosely, a portion or share of something. The Duchess argues that Queen Elizabeth's grief is only a fraction — a moiety — of her own, because Elizabeth has lost only a husband, while she (the Duchess) has lost both a husband (long dead) and two sons.
detail: From Old French moitie (from Latin medietas, 'middle, half'), 'moiety' was standard legal and poetic vocabulary in the sixteenth century, appearing in contracts, wills, and verse. The Duchess's arithmetic of grief — which she spells out in the lines that follow (TLN 1295-1298) — is the extreme stylization of competitive mourning that characterizes the play's lament scenes. 'Overgo' means 'to surpass, exceed,' another archaism the student needs.

The gloss of 'moiety' as a portion/half is accurate and the competitive arithmetic of grief that follows at TLN 1295-1298 is directly in the text.

anchor_text: All springs reduce their currents to mine eyes, That I, being govern'd by the watery moon, May send forth plenteous tears to drown the world
summary: Elizabeth imagines every spring and river flowing into her eyes so that, governed by the moon, she can weep a flood to drown the world. The moon was believed to govern the tides, the humours, and in particular the fluid balance of the body — a woman in grief could thus claim a special, cosmological licence for tears.
detail: Elizabethan medicine inherited from Galen the doctrine of four humours — blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile — whose balance determined health and emotion. The phlegmatic or watery humour was associated with coolness, moisture, and the moon; tears were its overflow. The moon's pull on tides (and, by extension, on bodily fluids) was standard natural philosophy — not merely a poetic conceit. 'Springs' here means sources of running water, not the season. Elizabeth's hyperbole is formally symmetrical: springs flowing into her, she then overflows to drown the world — a double inundation that mirrors the Noachic flood as a figure for catastrophic grief. The same moon-and-tears cluster appears in Richard II and throughout the play's sustained female lament tradition.

The moon-governs-tides-and-bodily-fluids reading is a genuine Galenic and Elizabethan natural philosophy commonplace, and the text explicitly says 'govern'd by the watery moon,' making the cultural context gloss textually grounded.

anchor_text: make me die a good old man! That is the butt end of a mother's blessing
summary: In an aside, Richard mocks the Duchess's blessing. 'Butt end' means the thick, blunt trailing end of something — the handle-end of a weapon, or the remainder of what is used up. Richard pretends to add the one wish his mother supposedly 'forgot': that he should die in peace. The joke is darkly sardonic — he knows his violence makes a peaceful death impossible.
detail: The pun has two edges. 'Butt end' literally means the thick end of a spear, musket, or other weapon — the part held in the hand, or the stub left over. Richard implies that the only 'blessing' left over from a mother's conventional prayer (love, charity, obedience, duty) is the belated wish for a good death. He then adds, with mock surprise, that he 'marvels' she forgot to include it. The sardonic register is characteristic of Richard's aside-humour: he treats every sincere human gesture — here maternal love — as a performance to be seen through. 'Die a good old man' simultaneously reminds the audience that Richard will do exactly the opposite.

'Butt end' as the thick or remaining stub end is accurate, and the sardonic register of the aside — Richard adding the one wish his mother 'forgot' — is clearly borne out by TLN 1325 ('I marvel that her grace did leave it out').

anchor_text: Though we have spent our harvest of this king, We are to reap the harvest of his son
summary: Buckingham urges the court to look past grief to the coming reign of the young prince: Edward IV was one harvest, now gathered; his son Edward V is the next crop to be reaped. For Richard, who stands just behind this reassurance, the agricultural metaphor signals the opposite of what it promises: a harvest is cut down and consumed.
detail: The metaphor of a king or reign as a harvest to be gathered recurs throughout the history plays, drawing on the Parable of the Wheat and Tares (Matthew 13:24-30) and on Ecclesiastes 3:2 ('a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted,' Geneva 1599). Buckingham's intent is to redirect mourning toward the future, but his language — 'spent,' 'reap' — carries an agricultural violence that the play's ironic context amplifies: the harvest of the new king will indeed be 'reaped' by Richard and Buckingham. The speech functions as dramatic irony, since the audience knows Buckingham is Richard's co-conspirator.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1329

The harvest metaphor is explicit in the text and the dramatic irony reading — that a harvest is cut down and consumed, foreshadowing Edward V's fate — is defensible; the Buckingham-as-co-conspirator context is established earlier in the play.

anchor_text: the estate is green and yet ungovern'd
summary: 'Estate' here means the realm or the state of the kingdom, not private property. 'Green' means immature, untested, fresh — the realm lacks a properly established king and is therefore vulnerable. Buckingham argues that exactly this fragility makes a small escort for the new prince safer: a large armed train might reignite the factional wounds that have barely healed.
detail: The word 'estate' (from Old French estat, Latin status) regularly meant 'the commonwealth, the body politic' in Tudor political writing — compare 'the estate of the realm' as a legal phrase. 'Green' as a modifier meaning 'raw, unripe, inexperienced' is common in Shakespeare (the 'green' wound of TLN 1339, the 'green' compact of TLN 1349). Buckingham's imagery thus sustains the organic/agricultural metaphor of his 'harvest' lines (TLN 1329-1330): the new reign is unripe growth that must not be agitated before it takes root. For the audience, every reasonable-sounding argument Buckingham makes is suspect because he has already told Richard (in the play's opening movement) that he is working to secure Richard's path to the crown.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1341

'Estate' as the body politic and 'green' as immature/untested are both accurate Tudor readings, and the organic continuity with Buckingham's harvest metaphor at TLN 1329-1330 is present in the text itself (Rivers echoes 'green' at TLN 1349).

anchor_text: As index to the story we late talk'd of, To part the queen's proud kindred from the Prince
summary: In Tudor usage, an 'index' was a table of contents placed at the beginning of a book — not the alphabetical index at the back that modern readers expect. Buckingham says the journey to Ludlow will serve as a preface or opening move in the larger plot he and Richard have already discussed: separating the young prince from the Woodville family (his mother's relatives) who currently surround him.
detail: The word comes from Latin index (something that points to, from indicare, 'to point out'). Early printed books placed summaries or tables at the front, so 'index' could mean 'preface, introduction, or pointer to what follows.' Here Buckingham casts the escort mission as the first chapter of a story whose full plan Richard already knows: to neutralize the queen's faction (Rivers, Grey) before they can consolidate power around the new prince. The metaphor of the story with an index is itself apt in a play so self-consciously theatrical — events are chapters in a plot the audience is watching unfold. The phrase also confirms that the two men's private scheming predates everything the audience has witnessed in this scene.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1362

OED s.v. 'index' n. does record a sense of 'table of contents, preface, or prologue placed at the front of a book' current in the 16th-17th centuries, confirmed by Shakespeare's own use of 'index' in this sense in Troilus and Cressida and Othello.

The Tudor sense of 'index' as a front-matter table of contents rather than a back-of-book index is well documented, and using it to mean a preface or opening move to the plot is a sound and unforced reading.

anchor_text: My other self, my counsel's consistory, My oracle, my prophet
summary: Richard lavishes Buckingham with three linked titles: 'my other self' (my alter ego, the person who thinks as I think), 'my counsel's consistory' (the council-chamber of my private deliberations — a 'consistory' was the formal assembly of a church council or court), and 'my oracle, my prophet' (the one who sees into the future on my behalf). All three are Richard's way of flattering Buckingham into thinking himself indispensable — just as Buckingham truly believes.
detail: A 'consistory' (from Latin consistorium) was the formal assembly where the Pope and cardinals deliberated, or any solemn ecclesiastical court. In English secular usage it could mean any formal deliberating body. Richard's phrase 'my counsel's consistory' thus means 'the court that hears and decides the business of my secret plans.' The three-fold apostrophe — 'my other self... my counsel's consistory... my oracle, my prophet' — is an example of climax (a rhetorical figure in which successive terms intensify the idea) working in reverse: the register moves from philosophical intimacy ('other self') through institutional gravity ('consistory') to religious awe ('oracle'). The effect is grandiose and, given what the audience knows about Richard's later treatment of Buckingham, deeply ironic: Buckingham will be dropped the moment he hesitates.

'Consistory' as a formal deliberating council is accurate, and the ironic foreshadowing of Buckingham's later abandonment is defensible given the play's overall arc, though calling the rhetorical figure 'climax working in reverse' is a minor stretch — the three terms intensify rather than diminish.

anchor_text: Woe to that land that's govern'd by a child
summary: The Third Citizen quotes a proverbial maxim that echoes Ecclesiastes 10:16 — 'Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child' (Geneva 1599). The young Prince of Wales (the future Edward V) is only twelve years old, and with powerful, rival uncles — the Woodvilles on his mother's side and the dangerous Duke of Gloucester — that minority makes the realm terrifyingly vulnerable.
detail: Ecclesiastes 10:16-17 sets the formula: woe to the land ruled by a child, happiness to the land whose king is 'the son of nobles' who rules soberly. Shakespeare's audiences knew the Geneva Bible text; the Citizen needs no further argument. The same anxiety drove Parliament to appoint Lord Protectors (Gloucester in 1 Henry VI, Humphrey in 2 Henry VI) during the minority of Henry VI — a precedent the Third Citizen is silently invoking when he warns that Edward V's reign may repeat those disasters. The citation of Henry VI's infant coronation at lines 1385-86 makes the parallel explicit: the last child-king's reign brought forty years of civil war.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Ecclesiastes 10:16 (Geneva 1599): 'Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a childe, and thy princes eate in the morning.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1380

Geneva Bible 1599 Ecclesiastes 10:16 reads 'Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child' (original spelling 'childe') — the annotation's quoted text is accurate in substance and the verse genuinely supports the claim.

Ecclesiastes 10:16 is the standard proverbial source for this formula, the Henry VI parallel is explicitly made at lines 1385-86, and the reading of the Woodville/Gloucester threat as the referent of 'child' is mainstream.

anchor_text: Henry the Sixth Was crown'd in Paris but at nine months old
summary: Henry VI was crowned King of England in 1422, when he was less than a year old, and later (1431) crowned King of France in Paris. His long minority — managed first by the Duke of Bedford in France and 'good Duke Humphrey' in England — was marked by faction, the loss of France, and ultimately the Wars of the Roses. The First Citizen invokes him as a precedent to calm fears; the Third Citizen will immediately demolish the comparison.
detail: Henry VI became king on 31 August 1422 at nine months old, and his minority lasted until the 1430s. The double regency — Bedford abroad and Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, at home — was turbulent. Shakespeare had dramatised those very factional quarrels in the Henry VI trilogy, so the audience recognises the parallel instantly. The Third Citizen's counter-point (lines 1387-1395) is that Henry VI had 'virtuous uncles,' implying that Edward V has the opposite: a 'haught and proud' mother's kin (the Woodvilles) and the dangerous Gloucester. Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) is the source for Henry VI's coronation dates.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on Henry VI's accession at nine months (31 August 1422) and his coronation at Paris (16 December 1431).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1385

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) is a real source that covers Henry VI's accession and Paris coronation; the 16 December 1431 date is confirmed, and the 'nine months' age claim is within the range of attested sources (some say eight, some nine months depending on rounding).

The dramatic interpretation is sound, but Shakespeare's line ('crown'd in Paris but at nine months old') conflates Henry VI's English accession (nine months, 1422) with his later Paris coronation (1431, aged about nine); the annotation's detail section lists both dates without flagging that the line itself is historically compressed, which slightly misrepresents what Shakespeare wrote versus what history records.

anchor_text: emulation who shall now be nearest Will touch us all too near
summary: 'Emulation' here means envious rivalry for power and pre-eminence — specifically the competition between the Woodvilles (the queen's family) and Gloucester for control of the young king. 'Touch us all too near' means it will hurt ordinary people deeply. The Third Citizen is warning that this elite power-struggle will not stay among the great; it will draw in and damage everyone.

anchor_text: When clouds are seen, wise men put on their cloaks; When great leaves fall, then winter is at hand
summary: The Third Citizen strings together four 'When... then' proverbs — clouds mean rain, falling leaves mean winter, sunset means night, untimely storms mean famine — in a deliberate rhetorical pattern called anaphora (the same word or phrase repeated at the start of each clause). The device hammers home one point: anyone who reads the signs knows a catastrophe is coming for England. It is the ordinary citizen as prophet, unable to stop the disaster but able to see it clearly.
detail: This passage is a controlled rhetorical performance. The repeated 'When' creates anaphora; the movement from sky (clouds) to trees (leaves) to the sun's setting to the harvest (dearth) is a descending natural order — the same 'great chain' logic that was the period's standard image of cosmic and political disorder reflected in nature. 'Dearth' means famine (a failed harvest), not merely scarcity; untimely storms that rot the standing grain were a genuine recurring anxiety in Shakespeare's England (the 1590s saw several harvest failures). The citizens' function in this scene is choral — they give the audience the plain reading of what the court cannot say aloud. Richard's succession crisis, like a storm, can be read in the sky before it breaks.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1401

The identification of anaphora on 'When' is correct, the 'dearth' gloss is accurate, and the choral-prophet function of the citizens is a mainstream reading; the 'great chain of being' framing in the detail is mildly over-interpretive but does not distort the core gloss, and the 1590s harvest-failure context is defensible background.

anchor_text: Small herbs have grace: great weeds do grow apace
summary: Richard quoted a proverbial rhyme at supper: herbs with 'grace' (virtue, goodness) grow slowly, while weeds shoot up fast. He was mocking the young Duke of York for growing quickly, insinuating that rapid growth is a sign of worthlessness. Young York grasps the insult but only recalls it belatedly, wishing he had shot back that Richard himself grew fast — and therefore, by his own proverb, must be a weed.
detail: The proverb was a common Elizabethan saying recorded, for example, in Tilley, A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries, H168: 'Ill weeds grow apace.' Richard's version adds the cutting contrast with 'herbs of grace' (a phrase also associated with rue, the herb of repentance, as Ophelia names it). The exchange is a miniature of the play's larger pattern: Richard deploys wit as a weapon, even at a family supper; the boy's counter-quip — that Richard must himself be a weed since he gnawed a crust at two hours old — is funny, but the Duchess's anxious silence underneath the laughter registers the real menace. 'Grace' here carries both the secular sense of charm or virtue and the theological sense of divine favour.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1429

The proverb reading is fully supported by the text: young York explicitly recalls Richard quoting it at supper to mock his growth, and the boy's counter-quip ('sweet flowers are slow and weeds make haste') shows he understood the insult; the gloss correctly identifies the 'herbs of grace' / rue resonance as secondary enrichment, not the primary meaning, so the reading does not overreach.

anchor_text: given my uncle's grace a flout / To touch his growth nearer
summary: 'Flout' means a taunt or mocking jibe — young York says he could have hit back at Richard with a sharper jeer about his own growth than Richard managed against him. 'Touch his growth nearer' means 'score a more cutting hit on the subject of his growing.' The boy is proud of the comeback he thought of too late.
detail: 'Flout' (noun, a jeer; verb, to mock openly) was in common Elizabethan use, recorded by the OED from the mid-sixteenth century. Here it reinforces what Queen Elizabeth calls the boy's 'shrewdness': he is sharp-tongued and clever enough to recognise that Richard's barb deserved a barb in return, and resourceful enough to find one. The scene prepares an audience to feel the full weight of this child's obliteration.

anchor_text: A parlous boy
summary: 'Parlous' is a contraction of 'perilous' meaning dangerously clever or shrewd — Queen Elizabeth calls her younger son a 'parlous boy' because his sharp wit has just produced a satirical joke about Richard's deformity, which is the kind of remark that could get someone killed. She scolds him for it ('go to, you are too shrewd'), then immediately warns that even small pitchers have ears.
detail: 'Parlous' was common in late-medieval and Elizabethan English as a colloquial shortening of 'perilous,' but with the added sense of 'alarmingly clever' or 'forward' (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'parlous': 'dangerously clever, shrewd'). The word had begun to fade from standard use by the seventeenth century, eventually surviving only in dialect. Elizabeth's reaction — irritation immediately followed by the proverb about pitchers and ears — shows that she grasps the danger; to joke about Richard's growth and early teething is to joke about the deformity he is intensely sensitive about, in a palace where walls have ears.

'Parlous' as a colloquial shortening of 'perilous' with the sense 'dangerously clever or forward' is well attested and fits Elizabeth's line exactly ('go to, you are too shrewd' confirms the shrewdness reading); the note about Richard's sensitivity to deformity-jokes is a reasonable inference from the wider play but is offered as context, not as the gloss itself.

anchor_text: Pitchers have ears
summary: This is a proverbial warning meaning small children hear and repeat everything — 'pitchers' are jugs, whose two handles look like ears. Queen Elizabeth cuts off the Archbishop's defence of young York with this proverb: it is not that she disagrees, but that the palace is unsafe for open talk, even harmless-seeming banter. The proverb doubles as an admission that anyone in this room might be a spy.
detail: The saying is recorded by Tilley (P358: 'Pitchers have ears and walls have ears') and its variant 'Little pitchers have great ears' survives in modern English. Its dramatic function here is sharp: Elizabeth's one-line exit from the conversation signals that the political atmosphere has become so poisoned that even a child's joke about his uncle — told in a room of female family members — cannot be spoken aloud without danger. It also retroactively sharpens Richard's apparent casualness at the supper table: he was testing, watching, noting.

sources.name: Tilley, Proverbs
sources.citation: M. P. Tilley, A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (1950), P358: 'Pitchers have ears (and walls have ears).'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1453

The proverb is correctly identified and Tilley P358 is the standard citation; the dramatic interpretation — Elizabeth shutting down talk because the palace is unsafe — is precisely what the one-line delivery signals, with no over-reading; the inference that Richard was 'testing, watching, noting' at the supper is a plausible extension but is kept in the detail section, not promoted to the summary gloss.

anchor_text: Lord Rivers and Lord Grey are sent to Pomfret
summary: Pomfret is Pontefract Castle in Yorkshire — a royal stronghold that had become associated with political imprisonment and death. Richard II was murdered there in 1400. That the queen's brother Rivers, her son Grey, and Sir Thomas Vaughan have been sent to Pomfret rather than to the Tower tells an Elizabethan audience that execution, not just detention, is coming. Queen Elizabeth understands this at once: 'I see the ruin of my house.'
detail: Pontefract (pronounced and usually written 'Pomfret' in Shakespeare's period) was a major Lancastrian stronghold in the West Riding. Its dark reputation derived above all from the murder of Richard II there in 1400, which Shakespeare dramatized in Richard II 5.5. The Woodvilles — Rivers and Grey — are the queen's kin, arrested by Gloucester and Buckingham at Stony Stratford when they were escorting the young king to London. Their execution at Pomfret is reported in 3.3. More's History of Richard III, transmitted through Hall and Holinshed, treats the arrest as Richard's first open coup, the moment he moved from intrigue to open force.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587): the arrest of Rivers, Grey, and Vaughan at Stony Stratford and their imprisonment and execution at Pontefract, 1483.

sources.name: More, History of Richard III
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (written c. 1513-18; printed 1557), on the Stony Stratford coup and the fate of the Woodvilles.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1460

Holinshed 1587 and More's History of Richard III (c.1513-18, printed 1557) both genuinely cover the arrest of Rivers, Grey, and Vaughan at Stony Stratford and their execution at Pontefract — all historical facts confirmed.

Pomfret as Pontefract Castle and its association with Richard II's murder (which Elizabethan audiences would recognise as a death-signal) is historically accurate and directly relevant; the claim that Elizabeth 'understands at once' is supported by her next speech ('I see the ruin of my house'); no anachronism or over-reading.

anchor_text: The tiger now hath seiz'd the gentle hind; / Insulting tyranny begins to jet
summary: Elizabeth frames Richard's seizure of power in two images: a tiger catching a 'hind' (a female deer, standing for the helpless royal family), and tyranny beginning to 'jet' — to strut arrogantly — upon an 'aweless' throne, one no longer held in awe or able to command respect. The predator-prey pairing collapses Richard's political coup into the language of hunt and slaughter. 'Jet' as a verb means to swagger or strut; it is now archaic.
detail: The tiger as an emblem of savage, unpitying ferocity was well established in Elizabethan writing (compare Margaret's 'O tiger's heart wrapp'd in a woman's hide!' in 3 Henry VI 1.4). The hind (a doe) conventionally figures innocence and gentleness: it is the quarry, not the hunter. 'Jet' (to strut, swagger) is recorded by Schmidt and the OED from the mid-sixteenth century, always with connotations of arrogance and display. 'Aweless' means inspiring no awe — a throne that has lost the numinous authority that should protect it. Elizabeth's speech (lines 1468-1473) is the scene's emotional turning-point, answering the intimacy of the domestic scene before the messenger with a sudden political horror.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon

anchor_text: themselves, the conquerors / Make war upon themselves; brother to brother, / Blood to blood, self against self
summary: The Duchess of York uses a series of paired, self-cancelling phrases — 'brother to brother, / Blood to blood, self against self' — to describe the horror of civil war: it is not merely war but a kingdom turned against its own body. 'Preposterous' in line 1482 carries its literal Latin meaning: 'with the last put first' (prae = before, posterus = coming after), i.e. unnatural, the order of things reversed — a civil war that inverts the order God ordained. The Duchess's speech recalls the Duchess of York's lament in Henry VI Part 2 and aligns Richard III with the full arc of the Wars of the Roses, which she has outlived.

anchor_text: I'll resign unto your grace / The seal I keep

anchor_text: queen your mother and your brother York have taken sanctuary
summary: Queen Elizabeth (widow of Edward IV) has taken her younger son, Richard Duke of York, into the sanctuary of Westminster Abbey — church ground where the law had no jurisdiction. Sanctuary was a recognized protection: anyone who reached consecrated ground could not be forcibly removed without violating canon law. She is using the church as a shield against Richard's power.
detail: The right of sanctuary in medieval and Tudor England was real and disputed: certain churches and precincts — Westminster Abbey most prominently — offered refuge to those who claimed it, and removing a person by force was ecclesiastical sacrilege. The scene dramatizes the tension between this ancient privilege and the political necessity Richard and Buckingham invoke. Holinshed and More both record that Queen Elizabeth took sanctuary at Westminster in 1483 with her younger son and daughters. The Cardinal's reluctance (TLN 1531-1537) and Buckingham's legal casuistry (TLN 1538-1550) reproduce the actual historical debate.

anchor_text: You are too senseless-obstinate, my lord
summary: Buckingham's long speech (TLN 1538-1550) is a legal argument designed to override the Cardinal's scruples about sanctuary. His logic: sanctuary protects those who have personally committed wrong or who have deliberately claimed its privilege; a child who has neither committed an offence nor knowingly claimed sanctuary cannot lawfully shelter there. The argument is technically clever and morally bankrupt, serving only to extract the prince for Richard's purposes.

The rhetorical strategy is casuistry — using the language of law and principle to reach a predetermined conclusion. 'Ceremonious and traditional' (TLN 1539) dismisses the Cardinal's appeal to precedent as mere habit. More, who dramatizes this scene at length, has Buckingham deploy similar arguments in his History. 'Sanctuary-men' (TLN 1549) vs 'sanctuary-children' (TLN 1550) is a neat verbal trick: the category of 'sanctuary-children' does not exist in law, so the concept itself is treated as absurd, which is the opposite of the Cardinal's position.

anchor_text: shall repose you at the Tower
summary: Richard suggests the Prince stay at the Tower of London before his coronation, framing it as the natural lodging place for a king. The Tower had historically been used as a royal residence before a coronation — but it was also England's most famous prison and place of execution. For the audience, who knows the princes will be murdered there, the proposal is sinister. The Prince's reply, 'I do not like the Tower,' shows his unease.
detail: The Tower of London served many functions simultaneously: royal fortress, state prison, treasury, and ceremonial lodging for monarchs before their coronation procession. Kings had indeed used it as pre-coronation quarters. Richard's offer is thus technically legitimate and simultaneously a death sentence. More and Holinshed both record that the princes were lodged in the Tower under the pretext of safety and that they progressively appeared less and less in public there before vanishing entirely. The young Duke of York's later line, 'I shall not sleep in quiet at the Tower' (TLN 1637), voices what the audience dreads.

The irony is terrible: a boy pondering immortality at the site of his own imminent murder.

anchor_text: So wise so young, they say, do never live long
summary: Richard's aside — spoken to the audience, not to the Prince — takes the familiar proverb 'so wise so young, they say, do never live long' and uses it as a death sentence he is already planning to carry out. When the Prince asks what he said, Richard gives a different answer: 'I say, without characters, fame lives long' (TLN 1575), pivoting the murderous thought into an apparent compliment. His comment in the next aside (TLN 1576-1577) explains the trick.

Richard's technique here — voicing his murderous intention openly, then immediately substituting an innocent paraphrase when questioned — is a structural signature of his character throughout the play. The proverb itself was proverbial in Elizabethan England, listed in collections of adages. Richard's variation on it is not the comfort it sounds: he is foretelling, not lamenting.

anchor_text: like the formal vice, Iniquity, I moralize two meanings in one word
summary: Richard names exactly what he is doing: performing the Vice, the gleeful comic villain of earlier morality plays, who spoke double meanings — one for the innocent character on stage, one carrying hidden menace that only the audience understood. 'I moralize two meanings in one word' means he just delivered two different messages with the same sentence: to the Prince's face, a compliment about fame; privately, a prediction of his death.

The Vice tradition was well known to Shakespeare's audience from popular plays of the previous generation, and Richard's self-identification as Iniquity is the play's clearest meta-theatrical moment before Act 5. It links to his earlier claim in 3 Henry VI that he could 'set the murderous Machiavel to school.'

anchor_text: Death makes no conquest of this conqueror
summary: The Prince's miniature oration on Caesar is a schoolboy exercise in the theme that brave deeds live on in fame after death. 'His wit set down to make his valour live' refers to Caesar's own writings — the Gallic Wars and Civil Wars — which preserved the record of his military achievements. 'Death makes no conquest of this conqueror' is a deliberate antithesis: the conqueror is himself unconquerable by death because fame survives him.

'With what his valour did enrich his wit' — valor furnished wit with subject-matter; the resulting writing immortalized the valor. The logic is the same as Sidney's in the Defence of Poesy: poetry (and writing) defeats time. The irony Richard relishes in TLN 1588 ('Short summers lightly have a forward spring') is that the boy theorizing about immortal fame will have no time to win any.

anchor_text: bring them to Baynard's Castle; Where you shall find me well accompanied / With reverend fathers and well learned bishops

anchor_text: to-day read o'er in Paul's
summary: 'Paul's' is St. Paul's Cathedral in London, whose outdoor churchyard and the pillars inside the nave served as the city's main public bulletin board. Official proclamations, legal indictments, and news were posted or read aloud there so the whole city could hear them. Reading Hastings's indictment 'in Paul's' is the official publication of his guilt to the people of London.
detail: In the sixteenth century the north side of St. Paul's Cathedral — 'Paul's Cross' — was the premier open-air pulpit of England, used for royal proclamations, condemnations of heresy, and official state business, often in front of large assembled crowds. The nave of the cathedral (Paul's Walk) was also used for posting bills and conducting public business. Shakespeare's audience would have understood 'Paul's' as shorthand for the chief public arena where official documents were disseminated. Posting an indictment here served as legal publication — the formal, public declaration of the charges against a man. The Scrivener's irony is that this solemn public procedure is being used to ratify a murder that had already been decided, not discovered.

This is the crux of the whole scene's argument: Eleven hours to engross the fair copy + the draft must have taken at least as long = the indictment was complete before Hastings was accused (or perhaps even arrested). Yet five hours before the reading, Hastings was 'untainted, unexamin'd, free, at liberty.' The timeline is arithmetically impossible unless the verdict was settled in advance. anchor_text: who is so gross That cannot see this palpable device! Yet who so bold but says he sees it not
summary: 'Gross' here means dull, stupid, or slow-witted (not large or obscene). The lines form a sharp chiasmus: everyone is clever enough to see the fraud, yet no one is bold enough to say they see it. Richard's tyranny works not because it deceives anyone but because fear makes witnesses pretend to be deceived.

The same dynamic governs the citizens of 2.3 who speak darkly of Richard's rise and then fall quiet, and the Mayor who endorses what he knows to be staged. The Scrivener, alone on stage, dares say what every Londoner knows. 'Palpable' as 'easily perceived by the senses, obvious': OED s.v. 'palpable' adj., sense 3: 'Readily perceptible to the mind; obvious, plain, manifest.' Compare Horatio's 'palpable hit' in the fencing scene of Hamlet. The speech is also the play's most compressed commentary on the nature of Richard's regime: it is maintained by performance, not by deception.

anchor_text: all will come to naught, When such ill dealing must be seen in thought
summary: 'Seen in thought' means seen only in the mind — kept private, never spoken aloud. anchor_text: his contract with Lady Lucy
summary: Buckingham claims Edward IV had secretly contracted (pre-contracted) himself to a Lady Eleanor Butler (also called Lady Lucy) before marrying Elizabeth Woodville, which would make the marriage bigamous and the children illegitimate. Whether the story was true is unknown and disputed, but it provided legal cover for the act that disinherited the princes. Shakespeare draws directly on More-via-Holinshed for this scene.

anchor_text: this prince is not an Edward! He is not lolling on a lewd day-bed

Buckingham is pretending to flatter Richard by calling him too compassionate toward his relatives — too good-hearted to depose his nephew — when every member of the audience knows Richard has already had that nephew's protectors arrested and killed, and is about to murder the nephew himself.

anchor_text: I may not suffer you to visit them. The king hath strictly charg'd the contrary
summary: Brakenbury, as Lieutenant of the Tower, has been ordered by Richard — who is now calling himself king, though not yet crowned — to bar all visitors from the young princes. This is the scene's first sign that the boys are effectively prisoners, not royal guests. The order anticipates what More and Holinshed report: that Richard systematically cut the princes off from family and loyal servants before arranging their deaths.

Brakenbury himself, in More's account, is the keeper who refuses to hand over his keys to Tyrrell until Richard issues a direct written warrant — the play stages this later. The moment when Queen Elizabeth asks 'The king! who's that?' and Brakenbury corrects himself to 'the lord protector' captures the exact ambiguity of the transitional weeks: Richard had not yet formally crowned himself, but was already acting with kingly authority over the Tower and its prisoners.

anchor_text: cut my lace asunder, That my pent heart may have some scope to beat
summary: Elizabethan women's bodices were tightly laced at the back; the stiff whalebone or buckram stays compressed the torso. When Queen Elizabeth cries 'cut my lace asunder,' she is asking to have the lacing of her corset cut so she can breathe through the shock. Sudden news was thought to cause fainting by compressing the heart — the same convention gives Juliet's Nurse her request in 'Romeo and Juliet.' It signals physical collapse, not mere distress.
detail: The tight-laced bodice was a standard feature of court and gentlewoman dress from roughly the 1560s onward. Medical and popular literature of the period associated over-tight lacing with 'the suffocation of the mother' (hysteria), shortness of breath, and swooning. On the Elizabethan stage, female characters — all played by men — used the convention as a vivid theatrical sign of overwhelming emotion; asking to be unlaced was shorthand for 'I am about to faint.' Juliet's Nurse ('Lord, Lord, she will be a joyful woman' / 'O, she is laced') and Imogen in Cymbeline use the same business.

anchor_text: A cockatrice hast thou hatch'd to the world, Whose unavoided eye is murderous

anchor_text: the inclusive verge Of golden metal that must round my brow Were red-hot steel, to sear me to the brain! Anointed let me be with deadly venom
summary: Lady Anne wishes the coronation crown ('the inclusive verge of golden metal') were a red-hot ring that would burn through her skull, and that the holy anointing oil used in the ceremony ('Anointed let me be') were poison. The speech turns the two holiest acts of a coronation — the placing of the crown and the anointing with consecrated oil — into instruments of execution. Anne dreads becoming queen more than death itself.

The anointing of a monarch's head and hands with holy chrism oil was the most sacred moment of a coronation, the act that conferred divine sanction (see divine-right-of-kings); to wish it were venom is to turn the sacred into the deadly. Anne's speech inverts the entire symbolism of coronation: crown = burning brand, anointing = poisoning. She is fulfilling the curse she laid on Richard's future wife in Act 1 — 'be thy wife... more miserable by the life of thee / Than thou hast made me by my dear lord's death' — as she recognizes that she herself is that wife.

anchor_text: as I follow'd Henry's corse; When scarce the blood was well wash'd from his hands Which issued from my other angel husband
summary: Anne is recalling the extraordinary scene in Act 1 where Richard wooed her as she followed the corpse ('corse') of Henry VI. The 'blood wash'd from his hands' is Henry VI's blood: Richard had just murdered him in the Tower. 'My other angel husband' is the Lancastrian Prince Edward, son of Henry VI, whom Richard had also killed at the battle of Tewkesbury (1471). Anne had been Prince Edward's wife; Richard killed both her husband and her father-in-law before courting her.
detail: The historical Lady Anne Neville (c. 1456-1485) was the daughter of Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick ('the Kingmaker'), and had been betrothed to the Lancastrian Prince Edward of Westminster, who was killed at Tewkesbury (4 May 1471). She married Richard of Gloucester sometime between 1472 and 1474; the exact circumstances are murky, but Shakespeare dramatizes Richard's grotesque wooing over Henry VI's bier in 1.2 as a demonstration of his power to compel any situation. By 1483 she was queen; she died in March 1485, probably of tuberculosis, though the play implies murder. The chroniclers follow More in reporting that Richard then planned to marry his own niece (Elizabeth of York) after Anne's death — a plot hinted at in the 4.2 and 4.4 scenes that follow.

anchor_text: never yet one hour in his bed Did I enjoy the golden dew of sleep, But with his timorous dreams was still awak'd

This is not a private marital complaint: the play consistently presents Richard's guilty conscience as erupting in disturbed sleep. His own nightmare on the eve of Bosworth — when the ghosts of his victims curse him — is the culmination of exactly this pattern established here.
detail: The motif of the tyrant who cannot sleep runs from Seneca's tragedies through Tudor morality writing. Richard's 'timorous dreams' in Anne's testimony anticipate the night before Bosworth (5.3), when he wakes crying 'Give me another horse! Bind up my wounds!' His own subsequent soliloquy there — 'I shall despair. There is no creature loves me; / And if I die, no soul shall pity me' — confirms the complete collapse of the self-assurance he has maintained throughout. Shakespeare also develops the topos in Macbeth ('Macbeth hath murdered sleep'), where sleeplessness signals the same unraveling of a murderer-usurper. 'Timorous' means trembling with fear, full of terror.

sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, 3rd ed. (1902), s.v. 'timorous': 'full of fear, fearful.'

sources.name: More, History of Richard III

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'timorous' is genuine; More's History does report Richard's troubled conscience, and the connection to the Bosworth nightmare scene (5.3) is an accurate internal cross-reference.

Anne says plainly that Richard's 'timorous dreams' (nightmares) wake her, and connecting this to the Bosworth ghost-scene (5.3) as the culmination of the same motif is a defensible structural reading; the Senecan sleepless-tyrant topos is legitimate context, and the Macbeth parallel is apt without overriding the local meaning.

anchor_text: he hates me for my father Warwick; And will, no doubt, shortly be rid of me
summary: Anne's father was Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, known as 'the Kingmaker' — the most powerful nobleman of the age, who made and unmade kings during the Wars of the Roses. He switched sides from York to Lancaster and was killed by Richard and Edward at the battle of Barnet (1471). Richard married Anne partly to claim her share of the vast Warwick estates; once those lands were secured, she had served her purpose. Anne says plainly that she expects Richard to have her killed.
detail: Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick (1428-1471), was called 'the Kingmaker' because he had helped Edward IV gain the throne, then turned against him, restored Henry VI briefly (1470-71), and was finally defeated and killed at the battle of Barnet (14 April 1471). His two daughters, Anne and Isabel, were the greatest heiresses in England; Richard of Gloucester and his brother George, Duke of Clarence, each married one of them in a notorious dispute over the Warwick inheritance. Anne's connection to the Lancastrian cause (she had been betrothed to Henry VI's son) was a political liability to Richard, and her father's rebellion was a permanent embarrassment. More's History hints, and the chronicles report, that Richard's treatment of Anne grew increasingly cold as her health declined; she died in March 1485.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the battle of Barnet (14 April 1471) and the death of the Earl of Warwick, and on the dispute between Clarence and Gloucester over the Warwick inheritance.

sources.name: More, History of Richard III
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III, c. 1513-18, on Lady Anne's position at court and Richard's treatment of her.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2405

Holinshed (1587) records the battle of Barnet (14 April 1471) and Warwick's death, and the dispute between Clarence and Gloucester over the Warwick inheritance; More's History covers Lady Anne's position at court — both citations support the claims made.

Anne's statement that Richard hates her for her father Warwick and plans to be 'rid of her' is exactly what the text says; the historical background on the Warwick inheritance dispute and Barnet is accurate, and reading Richard's motive as dynastic / proprietary rather than personal is the standard view.

anchor_text: Eighty odd years of sorrow have I seen, And each hour's joy wreck'd with a week of teen
summary: 'Teen' is an archaic word for grief, sorrow, or affliction — related to modern 'teem' (to overflow) and to the verb 'to teen' (to cause grief). The Duchess of York is saying that for every hour of happiness in her eighty-odd years, she has paid a week of misery. It is also a stark piece of arithmetic: she has outlived her husband the Duke of York, killed at Wakefield; her son Clarence, drowned in a butt of malmsey; and now watches her last son destroy what remains of the family.
detail: The word 'teen' appears frequently in Shakespeare as a noun for suffering: compare 'teen' in The Tempest 1.2 ('What torment I did find thee in!') and Titus Andronicus 1.1. Here it also participates in the scene's larger pattern of antithesis — joy set against sorrow, an hour against a week — which the women use throughout to measure how completely their lives have been defined by loss. The Duchess is approximately eighty years old if we reckon her as Cecily Neville (1415-1495), historically accurate; Shakespeare keeps the biographical detail to intensify the speech's weight.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'teen' sb.1: 'Grief, sorrow, suffering; trouble, affliction.' Primarily poetic and archaic from the sixteenth century onward.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2415

OED s.v. 'teen' sb.1 genuinely records the sense 'grief, sorrow, suffering; trouble, affliction' as primarily poetic and archaic from the sixteenth century; Cecily Neville's dates (1415-1495) are historically confirmed, making the 'eighty odd years' claim accurate.

OED 'teen' as grief / sorrow is correct, but the note's folk-etymology link to modern 'teem' (overflow) is not supported — OED derives 'teen' sb.1 from Old English 'teona' (injury, wrong) and treats it as unrelated to 'teem' (from Old Norse 'tœma'); retaining the gloss is fine but the etymology aside should be dropped or verified.

anchor_text: Pity, you ancient stones, those tender babes Whom envy hath immur'd within your walls! Rough cradle for such little pretty ones! Rude ragged nurse, old sullen playfellow For tender princes
summary: Queen Elizabeth addresses the Tower of London directly, as if its stone walls could hear and feel ('apostrophe' — the rhetorical device of speaking to an absent or inanimate thing). She calls the Tower a 'rough cradle,' a 'rude ragged nurse,' and a 'sullen playfellow' — grotesquely domestic images that make the massive fortress sound like a failed nursemaid. 'Immur'd' means walled up or imprisoned, from Latin 'in murus' (within the walls). The Tower was the most powerful symbol of royal imprisonment in England.
detail: Apostrophe was a standard figure of classical rhetoric (Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 9.2.38); Shakespeare uses it throughout for the highest pitch of emotional appeal, from Juliet's 'Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds' to Lear crying to the storm. Here the device works by the violent mismatch between the tenderness of the language — cradle, nurse, playfellow, 'little pretty ones' — and the stone fortress to which it is addressed. The Tower of London had been a prison for centuries; it held the princes on this very site, and by this point the audience knows they will never come out alive. 'Ancient stones' is not merely descriptive: it reminds the audience that these walls have seen royal prisoners before, and will again.

sources.name: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria
sources.citation: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 9.2.38 (apostrophe as the turning of address from a judge or absent person to the thing or person at issue).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'immure' v.: 'To shut in or confine within walls; to imprison.' From Latin 'in' + 'murus' (wall); in use from the late sixteenth century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2418

Quintilian Institutio Oratoria 9.2.38 does define apostrophe as the diversion of address from the judge to another target (adversary, absent person, inanimate thing), and the OED etymology of 'immure' from Latin in + murus is correct.

Identifying the address to the Tower walls as apostrophe is correct; the mismatch between tender nursery language ('cradle,' 'nurse,' 'playfellow') and the stone fortress is clearly the device at work, and noting the Tower's long history as a royal prison is appropriate historical context without overreaching.

anchor_text: do I play the touch, To try if thou be current gold
summary: 'Touch' is a touchstone — a smooth black stone used to test gold by the streak it left; 'current gold' means coin that passes as genuine. Richard is saying he will use this moment to discover whether Buckingham is the real article or counterfeit.
detail: Goldsmiths drew a metal across the touchstone and compared the color of the streak to known standards; the metaphor of testing fidelity by a decisive trial was proverbial. Richard has just been crowned and is now probing whether his chief accomplice will go all the way to murder. The coiners' vocabulary — 'current,' 'gold,' 'try' — fits Richard's habit of treating people as instruments with a cash value.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'touchstone' n. 1a ('A black or dark-coloured stone... used for testing the purity of gold'); s.v. 'current' adj. 7a ('in general circulation as money; valid, genuine').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2431
OED s.v. 'touchstone' n.1a and 'current' adj.7a are real entries with the glossed senses; the metallurgical summary is standard and well-supported.

The touchstone/current-gold metaphor is entirely sound: the test for genuine gold was a standard proverbial frame for proving loyalty, and Richard's framing of the princes as a litmus test for Buckingham's commitment is well-grounded in the text ('to try if thou be current gold indeed').

anchor_text: I wish the bastards dead; And I would have it suddenly perform'd
summary: Richard has already had Parliament declare Edward IV's sons illegitimate ('bastards') on the pretext that Edward's marriage was invalid. 'Bastards' is therefore not a slur here but the official legal label Richard arranged for the princes, stripping them of the right to inherit and clearing his own path to the crown.
detail: The bastardy decree was engineered by Robert Stillington, Bishop of Bath and Wells, who claimed Edward IV had been pre-contracted to Eleanor Butler before marrying Elizabeth Woodville; Parliament responded by enacting the act Titulus Regius (1484), legitimizing Richard's kingship. Richard now speaks of the princes in purely managerial terms: they are loose ends, not relatives. Shakespeare follows Thomas More and Holinshed in presenting this scene — Richard soliciting Buckingham's complicity in the murder — as the decisive moral turning-point of the reign.

sources.name: More
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (c. 1513-18), as printed in Holinshed, Chronicles (1587).

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Titulus Regius and Richard's solicitation of Buckingham.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2442

More's History (c.1513-18) and Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) are confirmed sources for Titulus Regius, the bastardy decree, and Richard's solicitation of Buckingham; the 1484 dating of Parliament's ratification is accurate.

The gloss correctly identifies 'bastards' as the legal designation from Titulus Regius rather than a mere slur, and the reading that this is a managerial rather than emotional framing is supported by Richard's clipped, transactional language throughout the scene.

anchor_text: thou art all ice, thy kindness freezes
summary: Richard uses a cold/warm antithesis: Buckingham's evasive 'your grace may do your pleasure' is read as frozen kindness — the warmth of loyalty turned to ice. The image captures Richard's impatience with anything less than instant, enthusiastic assent to murder.
detail: The metaphor works on two levels: ice as emotional coldness (Buckingham is pulling back) and ice as hypocrisy (the form of kindness without the substance). Shakespeare's Richard habitually reads hesitation as cowardice or disloyalty; the word 'circumspect' (TLN 2455) confirms that Richard interprets Buckingham's caution not as conscience but as the first sign that he will be useless. The exchange crystallizes the dynamic that ends the scene: once an ally ceases to be an unconditional instrument, Richard discards him.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'freeze' (to be cold, unresponsive, withhold warmth of feeling).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2446

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference work and the sense 'to be cold, unresponsive, withhold warmth' is a standard Schmidt gloss for 'freeze'; the rhetorical analysis does not overreach the source.

The cold/warmth antithesis for Buckingham's non-committal reply is straightforward and the text supports it; the claim that Richard reads hesitation as disloyalty rather than conscience is accurate to his characterization here ('High-reaching Buckingham grows circumspect' at TLN 2455).

anchor_text: converse with iron-witted fools And unrespective boys
summary: 'Iron-witted' means dull-brained, with wits as blunt and unyielding as iron — unable to read between the lines and ask awkward questions. 'Unrespective' means taking no notice, not looking too closely. Richard decides he needs simple instruments, not clever ones.
detail: The compound 'iron-witted' is Shakespeare's own coinage (its earliest recorded use is in this play). The pair of dismissals — iron-witted fools who can't think, unrespective boys who don't look — describes what Richard wants from a hireling: someone who will act without understanding or moral scrutiny. His next move is to find exactly such a person in Tyrrel.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'iron-witted' adj. ('Dull of wit, stupid'; first citation this line, c. 1594); s.v. 'unrespective' adj. ('Inconsiderate, heedless'; first citation this line).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2452
OED confirms 'iron-witted' first citation from this line (1597 first quarto of Richard III) and 'unrespective' is likewise first attested here; the Shakespeare-coinage claim is well-founded.

Both glosses ('iron-witted' = dull-brained; 'unrespective' = heedless/inattentive) are defensible and the note about Shakespearean coinage is plausible; the contextual reading — Richard wants tools who act without moral scrutiny — is firmly grounded in his immediate turn to hiring Tyrrel.

anchor_text: The deep-revolving witty Buckingham No more shall be the neighbour to my counsels
summary: 'Deep-revolving' means deeply deliberating or slowly turning things over in the mind; 'witty' here means clever and mentally agile, not merely funny. Richard is saying that Buckingham's very intelligence has become a liability: a co-plotter who stops to think is too dangerous to keep inside the circle of power.
detail: The phrase is tinged with grudging respect: Richard acknowledges that Buckingham is the cleverest man he has worked with. The turn of the scene is sharp — Richard hired Tyrrel before Buckingham has finished deliberating, and when Buckingham re-enters to beg his promised reward Richard stonewalls him entirely. The phrase 'neighbour to my counsels' (not privy to, not inside, but merely adjacent) signals how far the demotion has already happened in Richard's mind.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'deep-revolving' (meditating profoundly; s.v. 'witty' adj. 4, 'clever, shrewd' — the sense dominant in Shakespeare, distinct from the modern narrow sense of humorous).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2467
OED s.v. 'deep-revolving' (meditating profoundly) and 'witty' adj.4 (clever, shrewd) are real senses; the distinction from the modern humorous sense is standard OED guidance.

'Deep-revolving' as profoundly deliberating and 'witty' as clever/shrewd (not comic) are both standard Shakespearean senses, and the reading that Buckingham's intelligence has become a liability follows directly from the text and Richard's immediate action of recruiting Tyrrel instead.

anchor_text: The Marquis Dorset, as I hear, is fled To Richmond
summary: Thomas Grey, Marquess of Dorset, was Queen Elizabeth Woodville's eldest son by her first marriage and therefore the princes' half-brother. His flight to Henry Tudor in Brittany signals that even members of the Woodville family — Richard's own political network — are defecting to the rival claimant.
detail: Dorset was warned by his mother, who could see that Richard's favor was fatal for those connected to the princes. His flight to Richmond in Brittany (the historical refuge before the 1485 invasion) is the first concrete sign in this scene that Richard's position, though outwardly triumphant, is already eroding. Richard's response — not to pursue Dorset but to warn Stanley about his wife (Lady Margaret Beaufort, Richmond's mother) who might send letters — shows his intelligence network is working but stretched.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Dorset's flight to join Richmond in Brittany.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2473
Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) is confirmed to record Dorset's flight to join Richmond in Brittany; the detail is accurate to the historical record.

The identification of Dorset as Elizabeth Woodville's son by her first marriage and the reading of his flight as a sign of Richard's eroding position are both historically sound and well-supported by the dramatic context of the scene.

anchor_text: rumour it abroad That Anne, my wife, is very grievous sick
summary: Richard orders Catesby to spread a false report that Queen Anne is dying — the first step toward removing her. He intends to marry his niece Elizabeth of York to strengthen his title, and Anne must be disposed of first. 'Take order for her keeping close' means arranging her confinement so she cannot contradict the rumor.
detail: The historical Anne Neville died on 16 March 1485 of what was recorded as tuberculosis, but More and the Tudor chroniclers imply Richard either poisoned her or allowed her to die. Shakespeare follows that hostile reading. Anne's own bitter self-prophecy in 4.1 ('Lo, ere I can repeat this curse again, / Within so small a time, my woman's heart / Grossly grew captive to his honey words') has already prepared the audience for her death as a logical extension of Richard's predatory courtship. The plan to marry 'my brother's daughter' (TLN 2485) refers to Elizabeth of York, Edward IV's eldest daughter; the match would reinforce Richard's dynasty and neutralize her as a figurehead for a rival claimant.

sources.name: More
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (c. 1513-18); Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Anne Neville's death and Richard's plans to remarry.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2475
Anne Neville's death on 16 March 1485 is historically confirmed; More and Holinshed's treatment of Richard's plans to remarry and the implication of foul play are documented in both sources.

The reading that Richard is preparing the ground for Anne's removal to enable a marriage to Elizabeth of York is directly supported by TLN 2485 ('I must be married to my brother's daughter'), and the note that 'keep her close' means confinement is the correct interpretation of the phrase.

anchor_text: I am in So far in blood that sin will pluck on sin
summary: Richard acknowledges that each crime he commits draws him into committing more: murder leads to murder because each victim creates a new threat. The phrase 'so far in blood' echoes Macbeth's 'I am in blood / Stepp'd in so far' — a shared image of wading deeper into a current of bloodshed until turning back is as impossible as going forward.
detail: This is one of the play's few moments of something like self-knowledge — but it is purely strategic, not remorseful. Richard is not horrified; he is calculating. The syntax of inevitability ('sin will pluck on sin') frames murder as a logical chain rather than a moral choice, which is characteristic of the Machiavellian stage-villain who has dispensed with conscience. Compare Macbeth's fuller treatment of the same image (3.4.137-139), where it carries the emotional weight Richard consciously refuses here.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'pluck on' ('to draw in its train, entail').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2488

Schmidt's 'pluck on' gloss is plausible and consistent with his lexicon's usage; the Macbeth parallel at 3.4 is confirmed (line numbering at approximately 135-137 in most editions — the cited 137-139 is a minor edition-dependent variation, not a fabrication).

The gloss is sound, but the detail cross-references Macbeth's 'I am in blood / Stepp'd in so far' (3.4) as a 'shared image' in a way that implies direct influence or conscious parallel; Richard III predates Macbeth by roughly a decade, so the echo runs the other way, and framing it as a parallel rather than a source relationship would be more defensible — as written the comparison does not assert priority, so the reading is not technically wrong, but it risks misleading stude

anchor_text: those bastards in the Tower
summary: The two princes — Edward V and his younger brother Richard, Duke of York — are imprisoned in the Tower of London. Richard again uses 'bastards,' the official legal label Parliament has given them. Tyrrel's commission to enter the Tower and kill them is the scene's decisive transaction.
detail: The Tower of London was the customary lodging of English kings before their coronation, so the princes had been brought there in apparent state, not openly as prisoners. Their true situation — wards of a usurper with no outside access — makes the Tower, nominally a royal palace, their death-trap. The murder of the princes became the defining atrocity of Richard's reign in Tudor historiography; More's account (via Holinshed) names Tyrrel's two instruments as Miles Forrest and John Dighton, who smothered the sleeping boys with their bedclothes — a scene Shakespeare reports at 4.3 rather than stages.

sources.name: More
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (c. 1513-18); Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Tyrrel and the smothering of the princes.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2500
More's account (via Holinshed 1587) naming Tyrrel, Miles Forrest, and John Dighton as the agents of the smothering is confirmed; the summary accurately reflects what these sources report.

The historical and textual context are accurately stated; the note that the Tower was nominally a royal lodging and thus a disguised trap is defensible and adds genuine interpretive value without overreaching.

anchor_text: Henry the Sixth Did prophesy that Richmond should be king, When Richmond was a little peevish boy
summary: Henry VI was known for prophetic utterances, and the tradition that he had predicted Henry Tudor's kingship was current in Tudor sources. In 3 Henry VI (4.6) Shakespeare stages this prophecy directly: Henry touches the young Richmond's head and foretells his future greatness. Richard's reference here confirms the connection while his contempt ('peevish boy') signals how little he credits the danger — a dramatic irony the audience recognizes as fatal.
detail: 'Peevish' in Elizabethan English meant foolish, silly, or perversely childish — not merely irritable. Richard's dismissal is strategic (he must seem unafraid) but also genuinely characterizes how he misreads Richmond throughout: as a remote, negligible exile rather than a gathering threat. The prophecy Richard cites is part of the Tudor myth that cast Henry VII as heaven-ordained; by half-admitting it and then shrugging it off ('A king! — perhaps — '), Richard reveals both his anxiety and his contempt for providential thinking — the same contempt that marks the stage Machiavel.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Henry VI's reputed prophecy concerning Richmond; compare 3 Henry VI 4.6 (Shakespeare's dramatization).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2520
Holinshed records Henry VI's reputed prophecy concerning Richmond, and 3 Henry VI 4.6 is confirmed to stage this scene; both citations accurately support the claim.

The cross-reference to 3 Henry VI 4.6 is accurate, 'peevish' as 'foolish or childishly perverse' (not merely irritable) is the correct Elizabethan sense, and the reading of Richard's half-dismissal as dramatic irony is well-grounded in the text ('A king! — perhaps —').

anchor_text: call'd it Rougemount; at which name I started, Because a bard of Ireland told me once I should not live long after I saw Richmond
summary: The castle at Exeter is Rougemont — 'red hill' in French — and Richard's ear snaps on the syllable 'mount,' hearing 'Richmond' (which means 'strong hill' in French). The joke turns on a Welsh or Irish travelling bard's punning prophecy. This is the scene's moment of unguarded superstition: Richard, who dismisses Henry VI's prophecy, flinches at a pun.
detail: Richard is not really deflecting Buckingham's claim about the earldom with irrelevant rambling; he is revealing the anxiety that now shadows his calculated confidence. Prophecy haunts Richard III's world: the prophecy of the letter 'G,' Hastings's horse stumbling, Stanley's dream of the boar, and now this — a mounting series of omens Richard cannot wholly dismiss. 'A bard of Ireland' refers to the itinerant professional poets and prophesiers of Gaelic culture, who had a reputation in England for cryptic predictive verses; their currency was widely enough acknowledged that a pun on a castle's name could pass as a fulfilled prophecy. The historical Richard did visit Exeter in 1483.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Richard's visit to Exeter and the Rougemont anecdote.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bard' n.1 1 ('A poet and singer among the ancient Celts; among the Welsh and Irish').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2530
The Rougemont/Exeter/bard-of-Ireland passage is confirmed to appear in Holinshed's Chronicles (1587 edition, contributed by John Hooker); OED s.v. 'bard' n.1 1 is a real and accurate entry.

The pun on Rougemont/Richmond is the explicit mechanism of the scene and is textually unambiguous; the identification of the Irish bard as a figure of itinerant prophetic verse is defensible, and the reading that this moment reveals unguarded superstition alongside Richard's calculated contempt for prophecy is well-supported by the dramatic context.

anchor_text: like a Jack, thou keep'st the stroke Betwixt thy begging and my meditation
summary: A 'Jack' was the mechanical figure on a striking clock — a small automaton that hammered the bell on the hour. Richard insults Buckingham by comparing him to this mindless, repetitive mechanism: he just keeps banging the same note between the hours, interrupting Richard's thoughts exactly as the Jack interrupts the silence.
detail: The clockwork-Jack image is deliberately reductive: it strips Buckingham of agency and intelligence, reducing him from Richard's trusted partner to a dumb piece of machinery that strikes on cue regardless of context. The violence of the dismissal — from 'high-reaching' and 'deep-revolving witty' to a wind-up clock figure — measures the speed and totality of Richard's contempt once he has decided a person is used up. Richard's clock-metaphor also picks up Buckingham's literal question about the time ('Upon the stroke of ten') and turns it against him.

sources.name: OED
