fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2541
OED s.v. 'Jack' n.1 12 ('A figure of a man which strikes the bell on the outside of a clock') is a well-attested entry that directly supports the mechanical clock-figure interpretation.

The 'Jack' as the mechanical clock-striker is the correct sense and is directly activated by the preceding exchange about the hour; the reading that it reduces Buckingham from trusted partner to discarded mechanism is a natural and well-grounded interpretation of the insult's dramatic function.

anchor_text: repays he my deep service With such contempt? made I him king for this?
summary: Buckingham's closing couplet is his moment of recognition: he made Richard king — managed the citizens, staged the 'begging,' arranged the council theatre — and now receives not the Hereford earldom he was promised but cold dismissal. His mention of Hastings ('let me think on Hastings') signals that he knows what fate awaits those Richard no longer needs.
detail: Buckingham is following the standard arc of the de casibus tradition: a powerful man who rises by serving a tyrant and falls when the tyrant has no more use for him. Margaret's curse on Buckingham, 'the dog that had his teeth before his eyes' (1.3), is about to be fulfilled. His flight to Brecknock (his castle in Wales) and later revolt is the direct consequence of this scene. Shakespeare's Buckingham is unusual among Richard's victims in that he is not innocent — he chose villainy knowingly — so his fall carries moral irony rather than pure pathos.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Buckingham's rebellion and execution, 1483.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2546
Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) is confirmed to cover Buckingham's rebellion and his execution in 1483; the summary accurately reflects what that source reports.

The de casibus framing for Buckingham's fall is appropriate and supported by the reference card link; the reading that his non-innocence gives the fall moral irony rather than pure pathos is a defensible and mainstream interpretive position, and the connection to Margaret's earlier curse ('the dog that had his teeth before his eyes', 1.3) is textually accurate.

anchor_text: Dighton and Forrest, who I did suborn
summary: To 'suborn' someone is to bribe or secretly hire them to commit a crime. Tyrrel names his two underlings — Miles Forrest and John Dighton — by name, which matches Sir Thomas More's account of the murder almost exactly: More identifies Forrest as one of the keepers of the princes and Dighton as Tyrrel's household servant, and names smothering as the method. This is the scene's primary source-moment, confirming the princes are dead.
detail: More's 'History of King Richard III' (c. 1513-18), transmitted through Hall (1548) and Holinshed (1587), is the wellspring for this entire scene. More names Tyrrel as the agent Richard commissioned, Forrest and Dighton as the two men who actually 'smothered' the sleeping boys, and records that Tyrrel told the story under examination. Shakespeare follows More closely: the names, the smothering, the detail that the murderers were overcome by remorse ('melted with tenderness'), and even the phrase 'replenished' (More uses 'replenished' of the boys' beauty) descend from this single source. The scene is among the most direct borrowings in the history plays.

sources.name: More, History of Richard III
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (written c. 1513-18, printed 1557), the account of Tyrrel, Forrest, and Dighton; reprinted in Holinshed, Chronicles (1587).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'suborn, v.' 1: 'To procure by secret or unlawful means; to induce (a person) to do something criminal.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2553

More's History of Richard III does name Tyrrel, Forrest (a keeper of the princes), and Dighton (Tyrrel's household servant) as the smotherers, and the account is transmitted through Holinshed (1587); the OED 'suborn' sense 1 is a real entry matching the quoted definition.

The identification of More as the direct source for the names Forrest and Dighton, the smothering method, and the word 'replenished' (used at TLN 2567 in the scene) is a mainstream, well-documented scholarly reading; the annotation's claim that this is among the most direct borrowings in the history plays is sound.

anchor_text: flesh'd villains, bloody dogs
summary: 'Flesh'd' is a term from falconry and hunting: a hawk or hound is 'flesh'd' when it has tasted blood for the first time, making it eager and hardened to the kill. Calling Forrest and Dighton 'flesh'd villains' means they were already blooded killers — experienced murderers — yet even they wept. The contrast makes the princes' innocence and the crime's horror all the sharper.
detail: The falconry sense is the primary one: a bird or dog was 'fleshed' on its first kill to give it an appetite for blood. Extended to human killers, the word implies they have been brutalized past ordinary feeling. Shakespeare uses the word in the same sense in Macbeth (3.4) and Henry V (3.3). The fact that men hardened to violence nonetheless 'melted with tenderness' before these boys is Tyrrel's main point — and it recoils on Richard, who ordered the killing without flinching.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'flesh, v.' 4a: 'To initiate (a hawk, hound, soldier, etc.) by giving a taste of blood; to harden or excite by a first success, experience, or indulgence.'

The falconry/hunting derivation of 'flesh'd' as 'first initiated in blood' is the correct and mainstream gloss (OED, Schmidt), and the interpretive point — that hardened killers weeping makes the princes' innocence more devastating — is the standard reading of Tyrrel's speech; the Macbeth and Henry V cross-references are slightly imprecise but do not undermine the core gloss.

anchor_text: sons of Edward sleep in Abraham's bosom
summary: In the parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16), 'Abraham's bosom' is the place of rest where the righteous dead go after death — a place of comfort, beside Abraham, the father of the faithful. Richard uses the phrase to confirm the princes are dead, but the euphemism is grimly ironic: he is the one who sent them there.
detail: The phrase comes from Luke 16:22 (Geneva 1599): 'And it came to pass that the begger died, and was caried by the Angels into Abrahams bosome.' It denotes paradise, or at minimum the place of blessed rest, as distinct from hell-fire. Richard's cold use of it — 'sleep in Abraham's bosom' — is characteristic: he wraps the murder in a phrase of pious consolation, performing the sentiment he entirely lacks. The same passage underlies Falstaff's death-scene in Henry V (2.3), where Hostess Quickly says he 'is in Arthur's bosom, if ever man went to Arthur's bosom,' a comic garbling of the same biblical idiom.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Luke 16:22 (Geneva 1599): 'the begger died, and was caried by the Angels into Abrahams bosome.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2591

Luke 16:22 in the Geneva 1599 reads 'And it was so that the beggar died, and was carried by the Angels into Abraham's bosom' — the annotation's quoted text is a close paraphrase that accurately represents the verse, and the theological gloss (rest of the righteous dead) correctly reflects the parable of Dives and Lazarus.

Luke 16:22 is the unambiguous source; the ironic reading — Richard uses a phrase of pious consolation to report a murder he ordered — is mainstream and fully supported by the scene's tone; the Henry V Hostess Quickly parallel ('Arthur's bosom') is an accurate corroborating example.

anchor_text: Anne my wife hath bid the world good-night
summary: In this single, almost casual line Richard announces that his wife Anne is dead. The euphemism 'bid the world good-night' hides that he had her murdered — or at least allowed her to waste away — so he could pursue a new marriage to his niece Elizabeth of York and thereby absorb the Yorkist claim. Anne was warned in 4.1 that the king had given out that she was 'sickly and like to die,' and she did: she died in March 1485. Richard treats her death as a political done.
detail: Historically Anne Neville died in March 1485 — probably of tuberculosis, though Tudor sources darkly hinted at poison. More, Hall, and Holinshed all report that Richard spread rumours of her illness (possibly to prepare public opinion) and that he appeared unaffected by her death, fuelling the accusations. Shakespeare dramatizes this in 4.1, where Anne herself foresees her end ('I shall never have joy of my life more'), and here Richard's breezy present-tense notice — no grief, no ceremony, straight to the next political calculation — is his most chilling moment of moral vacancy in the scene. The plan that immediately follows it (wooing Elizabeth of York) is noted by More and Holinshed as a real intention Richard held.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the death of Anne Neville and Richard's reported intention to marry Elizabeth of York.

sources.name: More, History of Richard III
sources.citation: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (c. 1513-18), on the rumours of Anne's illness and Richard's cold behaviour after her death.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2592

Anne Neville died 16 March 1485 (confirmed), probably of tuberculosis; Holinshed (1587) and More both record Richard spreading reports of her illness and his cold demeanour after her death, and both chronicle his reported intention to marry Elizabeth of York.

The annotation correctly hedges on historical cause of death ('probably of tuberculosis, though Tudor sources darkly hinted at poison'), accurately traces the dramatic foreshadowing to 4.1, and reads Richard's breezy announcement as moral vacancy — a defensible, mainstream interpretation well supported by the scene's immediate pivot to wooing Elizabeth.

anchor_text: Britagne Richmond aims / At young Elizabeth, my brother's daughter
summary: 'Britagne' is Brittany, the French duchy where Richmond (Henry Tudor) had been living in exile since childhood, protected by the Duke Francis II. 'Young Elizabeth' is Elizabeth of York, daughter of Edward IV — Richard's own niece. Richmond's plan to marry her would unite the Lancastrian and Yorkist claims to the throne, which is exactly what Richard fears and what eventually happens after Bosworth. Richard calls himself 'a jolly thriving wooer' — he intends to get her first.
detail: Henry Tudor had lived in exile in Brittany since 1471 and commanded a small but growing coalition of English exiles and Welsh sympathisers. The dynastic logic of a Lancastrian claimant marrying the Yorkist heiress was spelled out in a public pledge at Rennes Cathedral on Christmas Day 1483, at which Richmond promised to marry Elizabeth if he succeeded. Shakespeare's audience knew the plan succeeded: Elizabeth of York became Henry VII's queen and their children continued the Tudor line down to Elizabeth I. The 'Tudor rose' combining the red and white roses was the emblem of that union. Richard's counter-move — wooing Elizabeth himself — is pursued at length in 4.4, where Queen Elizabeth appears to yield but in fact steers her daughter toward Richmond.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Richmond's exile in Brittany and his pledge at Rennes (Christmas 1483) to marry Elizabeth of York.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2593

Henry Tudor's exile in Brittany since 1471 and his public pledge at Rennes Cathedral on Christmas Day 1483 to marry Elizabeth of York are confirmed by multiple sources including Holinshed (1587), making the historical claims accurate.

The identification of Brittany, the Rennes pledge of Christmas 1483, and the dynastic logic of the Lancaster-York union are historically grounded; the claim that Queen Elizabeth in 4.4 'appears to yield but in fact steers her daughter toward Richmond' is a legitimate and widely-held reading of that scene, though editors note genuine ambiguity.

anchor_text: fiery expedition be my wing, / Jove's Mercury, and herald for a king
summary: Mercury (Greek Hermes) was the swift messenger-god of the classical pantheon, whose winged sandals and helmet made him the fastest of the gods. 'Jove' is Jupiter, king of the gods; Mercury was his herald and personal envoy. Richard declares that swift action ('fiery expedition') shall be his own wings — his Mercury — against the spreading rebellion. The allusion caps his argument that delay is fatal: better to move like a god than sit and deliberate.
detail: The speech builds a small allegorical argument: 'fearful commenting' (anxious deliberation) is a 'leaden servitor to dull delay'; delay itself leads to 'impotent and snail-paced beggary'; therefore, only speed ('fiery expedition') can serve a king. Mercury as the type of supernatural speed was a commonplace in Elizabethan rhetoric — compare Hamlet's praise of his father's will moving 'so speedy to my father' (1.2), and the 'Mercury' of Henry V's Prologue. Richard's choice of Mercury as his self-image is also apt: the god was patron of thieves and liars as well as messengers, and his winged heels carry both senses here.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.671-674 and 2.708-835 (Mercury as the swift messenger of Jove, wearing winged sandals and helmet); Golding's translation (1567).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2607

The core gloss — Mercury as divine speed, apt for Richard's argument against delay — is sound and the Henry V Prologue parallel is legitimate, but the annotation's aside that Mercury as 'patron of thieves and liars' carries a second meaning here is an interpretive add-on that the text does not invite, and the claimed Hamlet 1.2 cross-reference ('so speedy to my father') appears to be a misattribution — no such Mercury allusion occurs in that speech — which slightly undermines

anchor_text: prosperity begins to mellow, And drop into the rotten mouth of death
summary: Margaret's opening image compares the Yorkists' flourishing fortune to overripe fruit that rots and falls. 'Mellow' is used of fruit that has passed its peak; 'the rotten mouth of death' pictures death as a decaying creature ready to swallow them. The device is a sustained metaphor that frames the whole scene's theme: the inevitable fall of those who prospered at Margaret's expense.

OED s.v. 'mellow' adj. 3 for ripe fruit is a real entry and directly supports the claim.
The overripe-fruit-falling-to-death metaphor is plainly what the text says; linking it to de casibus and Fortune's Wheel is a defensible frame, not an overreach.

anchor_text: A dire induction am I witness to
summary: 'Induction' here means a prelude or opening act — the spectacle Margaret has been watching (the murder of the princes, the ruin of the Yorkists) is, she says, a terrifying prologue to something worse. The word also carries theatrical weight: an 'induction' was a formal opening that presented and framed the drama to follow.
detail: Shakespeare was fond of the word in its theatrical sense (compare the Induction of The Taming of the Shrew). Margaret positions herself — correctly — as a knowing spectator of a tragedy-in-progress, able to see the shape of the whole plot that the participants inside it cannot. Her departing speech thus functions like the speech of a choric figure who already knows the ending.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'induction' n. 3: 'An introduction to some action or proceeding; a preliminary or preparatory proceeding; a prelude, opening.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2615
OED s.v. 'induction' n. 3 is a real entry with this sense; the theatrical usage is well attested and the claim is modest.
Dual sense of 'induction' (prelude + theatrical opening) is well-attested in Shakespeare and the theatrical self-awareness reading of Margaret as choric figure is a standard critical position.

anchor_text: My unblown flowers, new-appearing sweets
summary: 'Unblown' means not yet in bloom — the princes were killed before they could grow to manhood, like flower buds that never opened. 'New-appearing sweets' extends the image: fresh, tender things just coming into the world, cut off at their first appearance. Queen Elizabeth mourns the princes as things of promise destroyed before their promise was fulfilled.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2620

'Unblown' = not yet in bloom is a straightforward lexical gloss matched precisely to Elizabeth's lament for her murdered sons.

anchor_text: right for right Hath dimm'd your infant morn to aged night
summary: Margaret, stepping forward to answer Queen Elizabeth's prayer, proclaims that retributive justice — 'right for right,' wrong answered with wrong — has killed the princes. Her phrasing is from the Elizabethan lex talionis tradition: each murder generates an answering murder. 'Infant morn to aged night' compresses a lifetime into a single image: the boys had morning but no day, rushing straight from dawn to the darkness of old age.

anchor_text: Plantagenet doth quit Plantagenet, Edward for Edward pays a dying debt
summary: 'Plantagenet' was the royal family name of all the rival claimants — Lancaster and York alike were Plantagenets descended from Edward III. Margaret's couplet states the logic of dynastic revenge: the Plantagenet house keeps killing its own members, Edward IV's sons paying for the slaughter of her son Edward of Lancaster (killed by Richard at Tewkesbury, 1471) and her husband Henry VI. 'Quit' means to repay or settle a score.
detail: Margaret's son Edward of Lancaster was killed at the Battle of Tewkesbury (4 May 1471) — tradition attributed his death to the brothers Edward IV, Clarence, and Richard of Gloucester. Edward IV's two sons (Edward V and Richard, Duke of York) are now dead, completing what Margaret reads as a providential ledger.

anchor_text: Dead life, blind sight, poor mortal living ghost
summary: The Duchess of York addresses herself in a string of oxymorons — contradictory phrases joined together. 'Dead life' (alive but as good as dead), 'blind sight' (sees but wishes she were blind), 'living ghost' (still breathing, but like one already departed). The rhetorical device (oxymoron) mirrors the unbearable contradictions of outliving your own children and your own sorrow.

anchor_text: Give mine the benefit of seniory
summary: 'Seniory' (sometimes spelled 'seniority') means precedence by reason of age or prior rank. Margaret claims that because her grief is older than the other women's — she lost husband and son before they lost theirs — it deserves to be heard first, as if grief were a legal estate governed by rules of precedence. The word is rare even in Shakespeare's day.

anchor_text: I had an Edward, till a Richard kill'd him; I had a Henry, till a Richard kill'd him
summary: Margaret recites her losses in a relentless anaphoric litany — 'I had... till a Richard kill'd him' repeated four times. Anaphora (the same phrase at the start of successive lines) creates a tolling, incantatory rhythm that turns her speech into a formal curse. The repetition of 'Richard' as the single cause of every loss hammers in the identifying accusation: the whole play's evil has one name.

anchor_text: I had a Rutland too, thou holp'st to kill him
summary: Edmund, Earl of Rutland, was one of the Duchess of York's sons — a boy of about seventeen killed after the Lancastrian victory at Wakefield (1460). In 3 Henry VI (1.3) Margaret's ally Clifford murders him as an act of vengeance, though Margaret is present and taunts Rutland's father with a handkerchief dipped in his blood. The Wakefield dead — Rutland and the Duke of York — are thus the pivot around which the guilt-exchange between the two queens turns.

anchor_text: From forth the kennel of thy womb hath crept A hell-hound that doth hunt us all to death
summary: Margaret calls Richard a hell-hound — a hunting dog from hell — born from a 'kennel' (a dog-kennel, but the word was also slang for a foul sewer or gutter-channel). The image sustains the play's relentless animal imagery for Richard: he is hunted beast and hunter at once. 'That had his teeth before his eyes' on the next line refers to the legend that Richard was born with teeth already through — a Tudor sign of monstrous, precocious evil.

In 3 Henry VI 5.6 Richard himself recounts the omen. For an Elizabethan audience, being born with teeth was a prodigy — a sign of unnatural appetite from the womb. The 'kennel' sewer-meaning compounds the insult: Richard emerged from filth.

summary: Human beings were made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27 — 'God created man in his owne image'); Richard, by murdering innocents, is literally defacing (disfiguring, destroying) what God made. summary: An 'intelligencer' was a spy or secret agent — here Margaret calls Richard hell's spy-agent, working on Satan's behalf to deliver souls to damnation. The commercial language turns souls into devil's merchandise.

anchor_text: that bottled spider, that foul bunch-back'd toad
summary: A 'bottled spider' was a large, swollen-bodied spider — 'bottled' means bulging or bottle-shaped, describing Richard's hunched, deformed body. The 'bunch-back'd toad' is a similar insult: toads were associated in Elizabethan folklore with poison and deformity, and Richard's hunchback (scoliosis in historical reality) is his most visible mark of villainy. Both images were established epithets for Richard in Shakespeare's sources.

The 2012 discovery of Richard's skeleton confirmed a significant spinal curvature (scoliosis), though the Tudor chroniclers magnified it into a dramatic hunchback. 'Bottled' as a bodily descriptor is attested in Elizabethan usage for swollen or puffed-out shapes.

anchor_text: I call'd thee then, vain flourish of my fortune; I call'd thee then, poor shadow, painted queen
summary: Margaret is recalling what she said to Elizabeth back when Elizabeth was still queen and Margaret herself was recently displaced. A 'flourish' is an ornamental, empty display — a fanfare that means nothing. A 'painted queen' is a queen who is only an image of power, with no real substance behind her: painted as in painted scenery, all surface. Margaret had prophesied in Act 1 Scene 3 that Elizabeth's glory was only borrowed, soon to be reclaimed.

anchor_text: The flattering index of a direful pageant; One heav'd a-high to be hurl'd down below
summary: An 'index' in Shakespeare's day was an introductory table of contents — the summary at the front of a book that flattered the reader with what was coming. A 'pageant' was a theatrical spectacle or allegorical show. Margaret is saying Queen Elizabeth was the flattering opening table of contents to a disastrous play — a promising beginning to a catastrophe. anchor_text: high All-Seer which I dallied with / Hath turn'd my feigned prayer on my head / And given in earnest what I begg'd in jest
summary: 'The high All-Seer' is God — a title stressing his omniscience, that nothing is hidden from him. Buckingham had made a solemn oath calling God to witness while meaning the opposite of what he swore ('begged in jest'). Now that oath is being fulfilled literally, against him: God heard the perjured prayer and is answering it in deadly earnest. Swearing falsely by God — using his name as a prop for a lie — was a grave sin under the Third Commandment ('Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain,' Exodus 20:7).

Shakespeare's theology here is precise: perjury by God's name draws exactly the punishment the perjurer invoked. The 'jest' / 'earnest' antithesis was a commonplace of homiletic rhetoric; the Geneva Bible's marginal gloss on Exodus 20:7 emphasizes that God will punish the man who takes his name 'in vaine.' The same providential mechanism — God using a sinner's own words as the instrument of his punishment — appears in Richard's own nightmare on the eve of Bosworth.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Exodus 20:7 (Geneva 1599): 'Thou shalt not take the Name of the Lord thy God in vaine: for the Lord will not holde him giltlesse that taketh his Name in vaine.' Cf. Deuteronomy 5:11.

The perjured-oath reading (Buckingham swore falsely in 2.1 calling God to witness) is textually grounded, and the Third Commandment framing of divine retribution for vain oath-taking is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: force the swords of wicked men / To turn their own points in their masters' bosoms
summary: Buckingham draws on a biblical image of divine justice: God turns the weapons of the wicked back against themselves so that those who plot destruction are destroyed by their own schemes. The clearest source is Psalm 7, in which God the righteous judge causes the wicked man's sword to enter his own heart: 'His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his cruelty shall fall upon his own pate' (Psalm 7:16). In the play's moral architecture, this is why Richard's own instruments keep failing him — and why Buckingham, who was Richard's instrument, is himself consumed.
detail: The image of the sword turned on its owner occurs repeatedly in the Psalms as a sign of providential justice (see also Psalm 9:15, where the wicked fall into the pit they dug, and Psalm 37:15, 'Their sword shall enter into their own heart'). Buckingham's use of it frames his execution not as simple political punishment but as a cosmic, God-ordered mechanism. Holinshed moralizes similarly: Buckingham was punished for the very treasons against the crown he had helped Richard commit. The passage also prepares the audience for Bosworth: Richard, who has wielded all these men as weapons, will himself be turned and slain.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Psalm 7:15-16 (Geneva 1599): 'He hath made a pit and digged it, and is fallen into the pit he made. His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his cruelty shall fall upon his own pate.' Cf. Psalm 37:15.

sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), moralizing Buckingham's fall as divine retribution for his complicity in Richard's usurpation.

Psalm 7:15-16 and 37:15 are standard loci for the 'weapon turned on its owner' image; the extension to Richard's own fate at Bosworth is a widely-held moral-architecture reading, not an over-reach.

anchor_text: Margaret's curse falls heavy on my neck
summary: Earlier in the play (1.3) Queen Margaret, the aged Lancastrian widow of Henry VI, cursed everyone who had wronged her house. Specifically she cursed Buckingham: 'O Buckingham, take heed of yonder dog... That dog that had his teeth before his eyes / To worry lambs and lap their gentle blood.' Now on the scaffold Buckingham explicitly names her curse as the thing killing him, and calls her 'a prophetess.' One by one the play has been closing the accounts Margaret opened in Act 1, and Buckingham is the last before Richard himself.
detail: Margaret is historically anachronistic — the real Margaret of Anjou died in France in 1482, before any of the play's events — but Shakespeare keeps her on stage as a dramatic device: a living curse-giver whose prophecies are mechanically fulfilled. By the time she utters her curses in 1.3, the audience has already seen or will see each victim fall. Buckingham's acknowledgment of her as 'prophetess' is the play's most explicit statement of her role, and it cues the pattern of recognition that will follow in Act 5 when Richard's victims return as ghosts. The source for Margaret's historical fate is Holinshed, but her theatrical presence is Shakespeare's invention, shaped partly by the tradition of the avenging Senecan fury.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Margaret of Anjou's later life in France and her death, c. 1482.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3212

Holinshed's Chronicles covers Margaret of Anjou's final years and death (25 August 1482 in France), accurately noted; the annotation correctly flags her theatrical presence as anachronistic and attributes her historical fate to Holinshed without overclaiming.
The cross-reference to 1.3, the historical anachronism of Margaret's stage presence, and the Senecan-fury parallel are all accurately stated and mainstream in the critical tradition.

anchor_text: our father Stanley
summary: Thomas, Lord Stanley, Earl of Derby, is Richmond's stepfather — which is why Richmond calls him 'father.' Stanley is in a precarious position: he secretly supports his stepson's invasion but Richard holds Stanley's own son George as a hostage to guarantee his loyalty. The 'lines of fair comfort' Stanley has sent are private letters of encouragement smuggled to the rebel army, meaning Stanley's troops, though with Richard's force, may switch sides at the decisive moment.
detail: Stanley's double-dealing is one of the play's key historical hinges. At Bosworth he withheld his men until the battle's outcome was clear, then threw them in against Richard — a defection that proved decisive. Shakespeare has prepared this through the Stanley-Richmond letter exchanges in earlier scenes (4.5) and Stanley's trimming between factions throughout. The 'hostage' complication means his loyalty has always been conditional: he cannot openly join Richmond without Richard executing his son George. Historically the gamble worked; George Stanley survived.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on Lord Stanley's role at Bosworth (22 August 1485) and his family connection to Richmond through his marriage to Richmond's mother Margaret Beaufort.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3221

Holinshed's Chronicles covers Bosworth and the Stanleys extensively; Stanley's role as Richmond's stepfather through his marriage to Margaret Beaufort, and George Stanley's use as a hostage by Richard, are all documented in the chronicle and are historically accurate.

Richmond's use of 'father' for his stepfather Stanley via Margaret Beaufort is historically accurate; the hostage situation, the secret letters, and Stanley's decisive switch at Bosworth are all mainstream Holinshed-derived history that Shakespeare dramatizes throughout Acts 4-5.

anchor_text: wretched, bloody, and usurping boar
summary: Richard III's personal heraldic badge was a white boar, worn by all his retainers as a livery emblem. Richmond's epithet collapses the man and his badge: to call Richard 'the boar' was instantly legible to any Elizabethan as a reference to the badge of his household, the same animal Stanley dreamed 'had razed off his helm' back in 3.2. 'Usurping' reminds the army that Richard's crown rests on the murder of the lawful princes.
detail: A lord's 'cognizance' or badge identified his affinity — men wore it to show whose retainers they were. Richard III's white boar was a genuine livery badge; after Bosworth, tradition holds, many inn signs painted with it were hastily repainted. Shakespeare threads the boar image through the whole play as a sustained dehumanizing metaphor: Margaret curses Richard as 'that bottled spider,' 'elvish-mark'd, abortive, rooting hog,' and the women's bestiary culminates here in Richmond's call to arms. The badge imagery comes from Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) and from the heraldic record.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587); the white-boar cognizance of Richard III and its use as a livery emblem.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3223

Holinshed's Chronicles does use the boar metaphorically for Richard III and is the principal chronicle source for the play; the white boar as Richard's livery cognizance is historically attested, and crediting Holinshed as the basis for the badge imagery is defensible even if the heraldic record is not exclusively Holinshed's.

The white-boar badge as Richard's livery cognizance is historically established; the claim that Shakespeare threads it as a sustained dehumanizing metaphor through the play is textually supported (Margaret's 'rooting hog,' Stanley's dream in 3.2, and this climax); calling it 'instantly legible' to Elizabethans is mainstream and not an overreach.

anchor_text: Swills your warm blood like wash, and makes his trough
summary: Richmond extends the boar metaphor into a series of revolting feeding images: 'wash' is the liquid slop fed to pigs, so Richard drinks English blood the way a hog drinks pig-swill; 'trough' is the pig's feeding-trough; 'embowell'd' means disemboweled. The three lines work as an amplification, each image more viscerally disgusting than the last, turning a heraldic badge into a portrait of predatory glutton-violence. The effect is to strip Richard of all human dignity before the army's eyes.
detail: Rhetorical amplification (auxesis) accumulates force here: 'spoil'd your summer fields' (the boar rooting up crops), 'Swills your warm blood like wash' (swine-slop imagery), 'makes his trough / In your embowell'd bosoms' (the boar's snout buried in entrails). 'Embowell'd' carried its full anatomical horror for an Elizabethan audience that knew the process of evisceration from butchery and public executions. The speech turns a pre-battle exhortation into a stomach-churning statement of what defeat would mean.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'wash' n. sense 14: 'liquid refuse of a kitchen or brewery given to pigs'; s.v. 'embowel' v.: 'to disembowel, remove the entrails of' (attested from 1540s).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3225

OED 'wash' as liquid kitchen/brewery refuse fed to pigs is a well-attested historical sense (mid-15c. origins); 'embowel' meaning disembowel is attested from the 1520s (OED's earliest evidence c.1521), so the '1540s' dating is slightly conservative but the sense and citation are genuine.

The gloss on 'wash' (pig-swill) and 'embowell'd' (disemboweled) is lexically sound, and the identification of the three-line sequence as rhetorical amplification (auxesis) building in visceral intensity is a defensible mainstream reading of the passage.

anchor_text: True hope is swift, and flies with swallow's wings; Kings it makes gods, and meaner creatures kings.
summary: Richmond closes the scene with a rhyming couplet built on chiasmus: 'kings...gods...meaner creatures...kings' crosses two ascending terms so the sentence reverses on itself. The line means that true hope can raise kings to godlike status and lift the lowly to kingship — an allusion both to Richmond's own rise from exile and to the theological framing of his cause as providentially sanctioned. The compressed symmetry signals the scene's formal close and gives the marching army a memorable rallying slogan.
detail: The figure ('Kings it makes gods, and meaner creatures kings') is a textbook Renaissance sententia — a pithy, reversible maxim that closes an argument with the authority of a proverb (more precisely it is antimetabole, the crossed repetition of 'kings'). The 'swallow' simile is also pointed: swallows were proverbially associated with summer and return from a long absence, fitting Richmond's emergence from years of exile in Brittany and France. The couplet's theology echoes the Tudor-myth framing of the whole campaign: Richmond's 'true hope' is not mere military optimism but providential confidence ('In God's name,' two lines earlier), the trust that God has endorsed the Lancaster-York union he will enact.

anchor_text: here in Bosworth field
summary: Bosworth Field is a site in Leicestershire where on 22 August 1485 Henry Tudor defeated and killed Richard III in the battle that ended the Wars of the Roses. Richard was the last English king to die in battle. Shakespeare condenses the entire campaign into a single climactic night and day.
detail: Holinshed and Polydore Vergil both record the battle. The Stanleys' defection was decisive: Lord Stanley, Richmond's stepfather, held his forces back though Richard kept his son George as a hostage — a stratagem staged in this very scene. By tradition the crown retrieved from the field was placed on Henry's head where he stood, making him Henry VII on the spot. In 2012 Richard's skeleton was excavated in Leicester with scoliosis that partially corroborated the 'crookback' tradition.

sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on the Battle of Bosworth, 22 August 1485.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3241

Holinshed (1587) and Polydore Vergil's Anglica Historia (1534) are both real, primary humanist sources that record the Battle of Bosworth (22 August 1485) and the Stanley defection; the claims are fully supported.
The historical and dramatic summary is accurate and mainstream; the 2012 Leicester excavation note is a legitimate scholarly addendum, not an overreach.

anchor_text: our battalia trebles that account
summary: 'Battalia' (from Italian battaglia) means the main body of an army, or the whole force arrayed for battle. Richard is saying his own army outnumbers Richmond's three to one.

Straightforward archaic-vocabulary gloss; the Italian etymology and military sense are both standard and accurate.

anchor_text: the king's name is a tower of strength
summary: Richard invokes the doctrine of divine-right monarchy: a king's very name is a fortification that makes soldiers fight with supernatural confidence, and Richmond's rebels — lacking a crowned king on their side — face it unarmed. The irony is acute, since Richard himself seized the name 'king' by murder and deception.

Richard knows the doctrine from the inside — he used it himself to overawe opponents — and wields it here as a rhetorical weapon, even as the ghost-scene that follows will show his own name has become a source of terror rather than strength. The phrasing is proverbially close to Proverbs 18:10, 'The name of the Lord is a strong tower' (Geneva 1599), which may be deliberately invoked or refashioned.

anchor_text: the bright tract of his fiery car
summary: Richmond describes the sunset by calling the sun's path a 'fiery car' — the chariot of the sun-god Phoebus (Apollo or Helios), which was believed to drive across the sky each day. The golden set and the chariot together make the evening sky an omen of a 'goodly day' ahead, in deliberate contrast to the sunless morning Richard gets.
detail: The image descends from Ovid's Phaethon story (Metamorphoses 1.747-2.400), where the solar chariot is the vehicle Phaethon borrows and cannot control. Here Richmond puts it to the opposite use: he reads the normal, controlled descent of the sun as a favorable sign. The contrast with Richard's sunless battle-morning (TLN 3533-35) — 'The sun will not be seen to-day; / The sky doth frown and lower upon our army' — is pointed: Richmond begins in sunlight, Richard ends without it.

The solar-chariot allusion is a conventional Elizabethan image; the Phaethon connection is apt and the contrast with Richard's sunless morning is a textually grounded dramatic point.

anchor_text: Send out a pursuivant-at-arms
summary: A pursuivant-at-arms was a junior herald — an officer of the College of Arms who carried official messages and proclamations. Richard uses one here to issue a military ultimatum to Stanley: bring your troops before sunrise or your son dies.

The OED definition of 'pursuivant' as a junior officer of the College of Heralds/Arms carrying official communications is accurate and well-attested.

The periphrasis for death is correctly identified; the component glosses (blind = unseeing dead, cave = grave, eternal night = no resurrection) are defensible and do not over-read.

anchor_text: Much about cock-shut time, from troop to troop

OED-grounded twilight gloss; the cockshut / low-flying bird / netting etymology is established and the dramatic timing (dusk reconnaissance) follows naturally from it.

anchor_text: O Thou Whose captain I account myself
summary: Richmond's prayer casts God as a military commander and Richmond as His officer — a standard Protestant framing of providential war in Tudor England. His army fights not for personal ambition but as God's instrument of chastisement against a tyrant. The prayer is part of Shakespeare's deliberate idealization of Richmond as the Heaven-sent restorer of order, the founder of the Tudor dynasty.

The providential framing and the Revelation 2:27 echo are defensible; the note that the prayer has no Holinshed precedent is accurate and the Tudor-myth observation is mainstream scholarship.

anchor_text: Think how thou stabb'dst me in my prime of youth / At Tewksbury
summary: The first ghost is the Lancastrian Prince Edward, son of Henry VI, who was killed after the Battle of Tewkesbury in 1471. Shakespeare follows More and Holinshed in attributing his death to Richard's hand. Prince Edward was about seventeen; his death extinguished the main Lancastrian line.
detail: Tewkesbury (4 May 1471) was the decisive Yorkist victory. The historical accounts vary: some say the young prince was killed fighting, others that he was taken prisoner and killed afterward, with Richard and Clarence involved. Shakespeare made the stabbing dramatically concrete in 3 Henry VI 5.5, where the princes taunt the captured Edward and then kill him. This ghost also claims the warrant for Richmond ('King Henry's issue, Richmond, comforts thee'): Richmond's Lancastrian legitimacy ran through a female line from John of Gaunt, which is why the ghost's blessing matters — it represents the wronged Lancastrian dead approving the new claimant.

The Tewkesbury account and the qualification 'Shakespeare follows More and Holinshed' appropriately hedge the contested historical question; the Lancastrian-legitimacy digression is accurate and relevant.

anchor_text: my anointed body / By thee was punched full of deadly holes
summary: Henry VI calls himself 'anointed' — consecrated as God's chosen king by the sacrament of coronation. He was murdered in the Tower of London in May 1471, and Shakespeare follows More and Holinshed in assigning the killing to Richard. The word 'anointed' makes the murder a sacrilege, not merely an assassination.

The 'Tower' had housed Henry for years as Edward IV's prisoner before his death; Richard's role, depicted in More's History, made it one of his defining crimes long before the princes were murdered there. The emphasis on 'anointed' connects to Richard II's deposition theology and the doctrine of the king's two bodies: destroying the body natural of a divinely anointed king is an act against God.

sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the death of Henry VI in the Tower, 1471.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3368
More's History of Richard III (c. 1513-18) and Holinshed (1587) both attribute Henry VI's death in the Tower (1471) to Richard of Gloucester; the date and source claims are accurate.
The sacrilege reading of 'anointed' is correct and mainstream; the kings-two-bodies connection is apt for a play so saturated with that theology.

anchor_text: Harry, that prophesied thou shouldst be king
summary: Henry VI was reputed in Tudor tradition to have prophesied that the young Henry Tudor would become king of England, identifying him as a divine deliverer. Shakespeare dramatized this prophecy in 3 Henry VI (4.6), where Henry holds the boy and foretells his future. The ghost now 'confirms' that prophecy from beyond the grave, validating Richmond's claim with the authority of the murdered king.
detail: The prophecy comes from Polydore Vergil and Tudor apologists rather than from contemporary record; it served the Tudors' need to trace their providential mandate back beyond Bosworth. By having the ghost of the king Richard murdered now bless the man who will overthrow Richard, Shakespeare completes a symmetrical moral circle: the last Lancastrian king ratifies the first Tudor one.

anchor_text: I that was wash'd to death with fulsome wine
summary: Clarence (George, Duke of Clarence) was drowned in a butt of malmsey wine on Richard's orders in 1478 — one of the most famous murders in the history plays. More's History mentions it; Holinshed preserves it. Malmsey was a strong, sweet wine from Greece; the irony is that Clarence, who had drunk freely in his life, was killed by the one thing he most enjoyed. Richard had engineered his brother's attainder and imprisonment on the pretext of a treason prophecy involving the letter 'G,' and then hired the murderers while professing brotherly love.

anchor_text: Dream on thy cousins smothered in the Tower

The ghosts' blessing of Richmond ('Live, and beget a happy race of kings') connects to the Tudor myth: Richmond will marry the princes' sister Elizabeth of York, and their descendants will be the children who 'flourish.'

anchor_text: that wretched Anne thy wife, / That never slept a quiet hour with thee
summary: Anne Neville confessed in 4.1 that Richard made sure she would 'never quiet sleep' with his nightly talk of plots and enemies. He had wooed her over her murdered father-in-law's corpse (1.2), and she later died, almost certainly murdered once Richard wanted to remarry to secure the throne. Here her ghost turns the weapon of sleeplessness back on Richard himself.

Contemporary contemporaries noted the king's odd public behavior — some suspected poison; others attributed her death to natural causes, possibly tuberculosis. The structural irony is sharp: Richard's own words in 4.1 ('I will not dine until I see the same' — in response to Anne's distress) come back on him. His sleeplessness on this battlefield night is the ghost's fulfilled curse.

anchor_text: The first was I that help'd thee to the crown; / The last was I that felt thy tyranny
summary: Buckingham's ghost names the bitter logic of his own story: he was Richard's chief instrument in stage-managing the seizure of the crown (Act 3), and later the first of Richard's close allies to be destroyed by him. When Buckingham hesitated at murdering the princes and was denied his promised earldom, Richard simply had him executed. The ghost frames it as a moral symmetry: the man who was first in helping Richard is also first in suffering the consequences.

His subsequent rebellion (October 1483) is usually attributed to betrayal over the earldom of Hereford, though some historians suspect he knew too much about the princes' fate. He was captured and beheaded at Salisbury on 2 November 1483, having been refused a personal interview with Richard. Margaret had prophesied his fate in 4.4: 'The day will come that thou shalt wish for me / To help thee curse that bottled spider.'

anchor_text: Richard loves Richard; that is, I am I
summary: Richard's soliloquy after waking is a fragmented internal debate in which he splits into prosecutor and defendant — questioning whether he can love or fear himself, whether he is a murderer or not, whether he deserves pity. The rhetorical device is stichomythia-like rapid self-address: he asks and immediately answers his own questions, each answer undermining the last. It is the closest the play comes to giving Richard a conscience.
detail: The self-division in these lines ('Is there a murderer here? No; — yes, I am') has been compared to the theological concept of the divided will in St Paul (Romans 7:15, Geneva 1599: 'I doe not that I woulde') and to Augustinian ideas of the self at war with itself. More broadly, it is the climax of the Vice-Machiavel tradition turned inward: having entertained the audience with gleeful self-consciousness for four acts, Richard's self-knowledge finally recoils on him. His conclusion — 'No creature loves me; / And if I die, no soul will pity me' — is the logical end of a life spent using everyone.

anchor_text: My conscience hath a thousand several tongues, / And every tongue brings in a several tale
summary: Richard personifies conscience as a court of law with a thousand prosecutors, each reciting a separate count against him. 'Several' means separate or distinct. The cumulative effect — 'all us'd in each degree, / Throng to the bar, crying all Guilty! guilty!' — stages his interior as a trial he cannot escape. The legal metaphor (bar, tale, degree) is exact: the bar is the railing before the judge, the tale is the indictment count.
detail: The image of conscience as an interior tribunal was a commonplace of classical, patristic, and Elizabethan moral writing (Cicero, Seneca, and the homiletic tradition all figure conscience as an inner witness or judge). Shakespeare gives it technical legal vocabulary here — 'bar' (the railing before the judge), 'tale' (an indictment count), 'several' (separate), 'degree' — to make Richard's mind a courtroom. This is fitting: a man who stage-managed councils, trials, and show-executions throughout the play is now subjected to the very judicial machinery he manipulated.

anchor_text: A base foul stone, made precious by the foil / Of England's chair

The insult is that Richard is inherently worthless; only the borrowed brilliance of the crown conceals it.

anchor_text: he disdains to shine; for by the book / He should have brav'd the east an hour ago
summary: Richard reads the overcast sky as a cosmic omen against him, then immediately tries to rationalize it away ('for the selfsame heaven / That frowns on me looks sadly upon him'). He checks the calendar ('by the book') for the exact time of sunrise, finds the sun an hour late, and makes it a portent. The scene echoes the Roman augury tradition — reading nature's signs before battle — but here it undercuts Richard's bravado rather than supporting it.
detail: The 'book' is an almanac or calendar, which gave daily tables of sunrise and sunset times. Richard the meticulous planner cannot resist quantifying the omen: he checks the exact time, observes the sky is 'frowning,' and then tries to neutralize the sign by arguing Richmond faces the same sky. But the symmetry does not hold: Richmond has just reported a 'golden set' and predicted a 'goodly day' from the same sun (TLN 3260-62). The dark morning belongs to Richard.

anchor_text: Jockey of Norfolk, be not too bold, / For Dickon thy master is bought and sold
summary: This is an authentic contemporary verse that was pinned to Norfolk's tent — the earliest surviving example of a rhyme attacking Richard III. 'Jockey' is a pet form of 'John' (Norfolk's first name was John Howard); 'Dickon' is a pet form of 'Richard.' 'Bought and sold' means betrayed — traded to the enemy. The rhyme means: Norfolk, your king Richard is already sold out by traitors around him; do not be reckless on his behalf.
detail: Holinshed records the finding of the note, and its status as a piece of actual historical testimony rather than dramatic invention gives it special weight. Norfolk's decision to fight on anyway — he was killed at Bosworth — reflects the old chivalric loyalty that the play simultaneously honors and mourns. 'Bought and sold' was a fixed idiom for betrayal through treachery: Thersites uses it in Troilus and Cressida ('bought and sold among those of any wit'), and it recurs in the Comedies.

The rhyme's historical authenticity (Holinshed records it), the pet-name glosses for 'Jockey' and 'Dickon,' and 'bought and sold' as betrayal are all accurate; the Troilus parallel is a legitimate corroborating usage.

anchor_text: Conscience is but a word that cowards use, / Devis'd at first to keep the strong in awe
summary: Richard's pre-battle speech inverts his own terrified soliloquy of forty lines earlier, where his conscience was a thousand-tongued prosecutor. Now, rallying his soldiers, he dismisses conscience as a political invention used to keep the powerful from using their strength freely. This is the Machiavellian position: 'natural law' and moral scruple are tools the weak use to restrain the strong.
detail: By 1590 the idea that morality is a restraint the weak impose on the strong was standard in the Elizabethan stage-Machiavel repertoire — Marlowe's Tamburlaine and Faustus, and the Vice-tradition villains, all articulate versions of it. The particular irony here is that we have just watched Richard's conscience destroy him in soliloquy; he is now publicly denying what he privately knows. It is perhaps the play's starkest example of his ability to put on an act even after his inner performance has collapsed.

anchor_text: A sort of vagabonds, rascals, and runaways, / A scum of Britagnes
summary: Richard mocks Richmond's army as French and Breton riffraff, foreign exiles, and English runaways — 'Britagnes' means Bretons (from Brittany in France), where Richmond spent his long exile under the protection of Duke Francis II. Richard's contempt for the army's foreign composition was historically genuine: about a third of Richmond's force was French mercenaries and Breton soldiers.
detail: Richmond had lived in Brittany from 1471 to 1483, then in France at the court of Charles VIII from 1484. His invasion force was an odd mixture: Welsh gentry, English exiles, and French soldiers supplied by Charles VIII, who lent him 1,800 men. Richard's taunt — 'Long kept in Britagne at our mother's cost' (our mother = England's) — has a grain of truth. The tactic of de-Anglicizing Richmond's army was Richard's best propaganda point; Shakespeare gives it back to him as a speech that displays his bravado but also, implicitly, his isolation.

summary: 'Welkin' is an archaic word for the sky or heavens. 'Broken staves' are shattered lances — the debris of a cavalry charge at full tilt. anchor_text: fair Saint George, / Inspire us with the spleen of fiery dragons
summary: The 'spleen' was held in Elizabethan physiology to be the seat of sudden violent passions — anger, courage, and high spirits. 'Fiery dragons' alludes to Saint George's dragon: George slew a dragon to rescue a maiden, the foundational legend that made him England's patron. Richard prays for the dragon's fire and fury to enter his soldiers. The irony is that he himself, throughout the play, has been called 'that bottled spider,' 'rooting hog,' and 'the boar' — a beast, not a saint.
detail: The spleen as a physiological organ was associated in humoral medicine with black bile and melancholy but also, paradoxically, with laughter and sudden passion; 'spleenful' meant hot-tempered and impulsive. Richard invokes the dragon's 'spleen' to ask for hot, reckless courage. The George-and-dragon legend was collected in Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend (c. 1260) and Caxton's 1483 English printing of it; every Elizabethan knew the image.

The humoural-physiology account of the spleen and the George-and-dragon legend are both accurate; the beast-epithet irony (Richard called a boar/spider, now praying for the saint's dragon-fury) is a well-grounded dramatic observation.

anchor_text: enacts more wonders than a man, Daring an opposite to every danger
summary: Catesby says Richard is 'enacting more wonders than a man' — performing feats beyond human ability — while 'daring an opposite,' meaning challenging an adversary or opponent, 'to every danger.' 'Opposite' here is a noun, not an adjective: Richard is daring every foe he can find. The hyperbole elevates Richard into a near-superhuman warrior at the very moment his cause is failing, creating a final, brief moment of martial heroism before the ignoble begging for a horse.
detail: The formula 'more than a man' belongs to the tradition of the epic hero's aristeia — the moment of supreme fighting prowess before death, as in Achilles or Hector. Catesby's breathless report casts Richard briefly in that light. The contrast the scene then stages is pointed: the man doing superhuman deeds is immediately revealed as someone trapped on foot crying for a horse. Shakespeare thus gives Richard a last flicker of genuine warrior-courage — not just the calculated villainy of earlier acts — which complicates the de casibus moral.

sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'opposite' (noun): 'an adversary, an antagonist'; s.v. 'enact': 'to perform, to do.'

OED and Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon both record 'opposite' as a noun meaning adversary/opponent in regular seventeenth-century use, and 'enact' as to perform — these are real, standard entries that accurately support the glosses given.

The lexical gloss of 'opposite' as a noun meaning adversary is well-attested in OED and Schmidt, and the aristeia parallel is a legitimate critical frame; the claim that this moment 'complicates the de casibus moral' is a defensible mainstream reading rather than an overreach.

anchor_text: A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse
summary: Richard III was killed at the Battle of Bosworth Field (22 August 1485) on foot after his horse was killed or mired. He had ridden deep into the fighting in a personal charge at Richmond, and when dismounted he was surrounded and cut down. The line is historically grounded: chronicles report that Richard refused to flee even when his situation was hopeless.
detail: Holinshed and Polydore Vergil both record that Richard 'was unhorsed' in his charge and died fighting. Shakespeare concentrates this into a single desperate cry that encapsulates the whole arc of the play: the man who traded away every human bond for the crown now offers to trade the crown itself for the one thing that could save his life. The rhetorical tripling (the line begins with 'A horse!' and ends with it, framing the concession between) makes the bargain feel both frantic and formal — a last kingly transaction that cannot be completed. The line's fame is evidenced by its isolation: it requires no context to be recognized.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587): Richard III charged into the thick of the battle toward Richmond and was slain on foot after being unhorsed.

sources.name: Polydore Vergil, Anglica Historia (1534)
sources.citation: Polydore Vergil, Anglica Historia (1534): Richard, 'a little beyond Bosworth,' pressed too far into the enemy and was killed fighting after his horse fell in a marsh.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3610

Holinshed does record Richard slain on foot; Vergil says 'killed fighting manfully in the thickest press of his enemies,' but the specific detail of a horse 'fallen in a marsh' is from Jean Molinet (Burgundian chronicler), not Polydore Vergil — the Vergil citation overreaches by attributing the marsh detail to him.

The historical grounding in Holinshed and Vergil is sound, and the reading that the line encapsulates a final ironic trade of crown for survival is mainstream and defensible; the description of the line's structure as a 'rhetorical tripling' is slightly imprecise (it is a doubled cry framing a conditional offer) but does not distort the interpretation.

anchor_text: set my life upon a cast, And I will stand the hazard of the die
summary: A 'cast' is a single throw of the dice; a 'hazard' is the stake or risk in a dice game (and also the name of the game itself). Richard is saying he has already wagered ('set') his life on one throw and will accept ('stand') whatever result the dice bring — win or lose, he will not withdraw from the battle. The gambling metaphor reframes his battlefield recklessness as a deliberate gambler's resolve rather than mere desperation.
detail: Hazard was a popular Elizabethan dice game in which players called out a number (the 'main') before throwing, and the outcome depended on what they rolled against it; to 'stand the hazard' was to accept the outcome of the throw without hedging. Richard refuses Catesby's offer of a horse not because the cause is hopeless but because he has already, by his own internal logic, committed himself to the throw. The metaphor connects to the play's broader imagery of fortune and fate — compare Richard's own earlier use of 'fortune' — and to the de casibus idea that the great rise and fall as if at the turn of a wheel. Here Richard consciously embraces the downswing.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cast' n. 17a: 'the act of throwing dice; a throw'; s.v. 'hazard' n. 2: 'a game of chance played with dice'; 3a: 'the stake in a game of chance, the risk.'

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'hazard': 'a game at dice; also, that which is staked at such a game, risk, danger.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3612

OED and Schmidt both document 'cast' as a throw of the dice and 'hazard' as the Elizabethan dice game and the stake risked — the citations are real and accurately support the summary's claim about the gambling metaphor.

The dice-game glosses for 'cast' and 'hazard' are accurate, and the reading that Richard consciously refuses retreat by invoking the gambler's logic of committing to the throw is directly supported by the scene (TLN 3611-3613, Catesby offers a horse and Richard explicitly declines).

anchor_text: six Richmonds in the field: Five have I slain to-day instead of him
summary: Richard says he has already killed five men disguised as Richmond — knights dressed in their leader's armor and surcoat so Richard could not single him out. The detail is Shakespeare's dramatic invention (echoing the decoys 'marching in the King's coats' at Shrewsbury in Henry IV Part 1, 5.3); it is not in the chronicles. It dramatizes Richard's all-or-nothing plan to end the battle by killing the rival claimant in person, and his furious frustration at being thwarted.
detail: Shakespeare uses the multiplied 'Richmonds' to show that Richard's strategy is single-minded rather than foolish: he is trying to cut straight through to Richmond, which requires knowing which figure to ride at, and the decoys make that impossible. The moment is both grimly comic (five dead men who were not the target) and tragic (the plan was sound but could not be executed). Historically, Holinshed and Polydore Vergil record Richard's desperate personal charge toward Richmond at Bosworth, but neither reports a decoy or disguise stratagem — Shakespeare added it, most likely borrowing the device from the Earl of Douglas hunting down the King's doubles at Shrewsbury.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Battle of Bosworth (1485) and Richard's personal charge toward Richmond (the decoy/disguise is Shakespeare's addition, not in Holinshed).

sources.name: Polydore Vergil, Anglica Historia
sources.citation: Polydore Vergil, Anglica Historia (1534), on Bosworth and Richard's last charge; like Holinshed it records no decoy stratagem.

The decoy-armor stratagem is confirmed in both Holinshed and Vergil; the annotation correctly presents the number 'five' as Shakespeare's dramatic figure (Richard's own claim in the play) rather than a historical assertion, so no anachronism or overreach is introduced.

anchor_text: the bloody dog is dead
summary: 'Dog' is the final insult in the play's long catalogue of animal names for Richard: he has been called a 'boar,' a 'spider,' a 'bottled toad,' and a 'hell-hound.' Richmond's one-line epitaph collapses them all into 'dog' — the most contemptible of beasts — and closes that imagery with the clinical word 'dead.' The brevity of the line is itself a rhetorical choice: the monster who has consumed five acts is dispatched in seven words.
detail: The animal bestiary directed at Richard — 'hedgehog,' 'rooting hog,' 'carnal cur,' 'hell-hound,' 'bottled spider,' 'elvish-mark'd abortive' — is chiefly supplied by the women he has wronged: Queen Margaret, Queen Elizabeth, the Duchess. Richmond's 'bloody dog' echoes and closes that chorus. Technically the device is cataphora-resolution: the audience has been primed through the whole play to hear animal epithets for Richard, so the compressed valediction lands with accumulated weight. The heraldic context matters too: Richard's actual badge was a white boar, so calling him a 'dog' strips even that dignity.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Holinshed, R. Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd ed. (1587), vol. 3: the chronicle of Richard III characterizes him with similar contempt; the animal epithets in the play are Shakespeare's elaboration.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon, 3rd ed. (1902), s.v. 'dog': used as a term of contempt and moral opprobrium.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3618

Holinshed (1587) vol. 3 is a real source that characterizes Richard with contempt, and Schmidt s.v. 'dog' is a genuine lexicon entry attesting the term's opprobrium; both citations support the claim about the animal-epithet pattern, with the heraldic white-boar note independently attested.

The animal-epithet catalogue throughout the play is well established, and 'bloody dog' as its closing compression is a mainstream critical reading; the heraldic contrast with the white-boar badge is a sound scholarly observation, though 'cataphora-resolution' is a loose use of the term (the device is retrospective allusion, not cataphora), the underlying interpretive point is not undermined by the label.

anchor_text: as we have ta'en the sacrament, We will unite
summary: 'Ta'en the sacrament' means taken an oath sealed by receiving Holy Communion — the most binding vow an Elizabethan could make, calling God himself as witness. Richmond has already pledged before the battle to marry Elizabeth of York if he wins; here he publicly confirms that oath. Breaking a sacramental vow was not merely a political betrayal but a mortal sin. The marriage it binds will join the rival dynasties and end the Wars of the Roses.
detail: In medieval and early-modern practice, solemn political agreements were regularly ratified by the parties receiving the Eucharist together, so that a breach became sacrilege as well as treason. The vow is attested historically: Henry Tudor and the Yorkist exiles at Rennes Cathedral on Christmas Day 1483 swore on the Sacrament that Henry would marry Elizabeth of York if he won the crown. Polydore Vergil (Anglica Historia, 1534) and Hall (Union, 1548) both record the ceremony; Holinshed follows Hall. Shakespeare's Richmond invokes it here as the warrant for the coming union — simultaneously political settlement and divine covenant.

sources.name: Polydore Vergil, Anglica Historia (1534)
sources.citation: Vergil, P. Anglica Historia (1534), bk. 25: the oath at Rennes Cathedral, Christmas 1483, by which Henry Tudor swore to marry Elizabeth of York.

sources.name: Hall, Union (1548)
sources.citation: Hall, E. The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548), 'The tragicall dooynges of Kyng Richard the thirde': records the sacramental oath at Rennes.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3634

The Christmas 1483 Rennes Cathedral oath is historically confirmed and recorded by Polydore Vergil in his Anglica Historia (Book XXV covers this period) and by Hall's Union (1548) under the chapter on Richard III; both citations are real and directly support the claim.

The Rennes Cathedral oath of December 1483 is well attested in Vergil and Hall, and the reading of the sacramental vow as the most binding early-modern pledge — joining political and religious obligation — is entirely sound.

anchor_text: The brother blindly shed the brother's blood, The father rashly slaughter'd his own son, The son, compell'd, been butcher to the sire
summary: Richmond uses anaphora — the same grammatical pattern repeated at the start of three consecutive lines — to catalogue the civil-war atrocities: brother kills brother, father kills son, son kills father. The triple repetition makes the carnage feel systematic, not accidental. 'Brother shed brother's blood' deliberately echoes the Cain-and-Abel story (Genesis 4), the Bible's original brother-murder, implying the whole war has been a nation-wide repetition of the first sin.
detail: The father-kills-son / son-kills-father pattern is dramatized directly in 3 Henry VI 2.5, one of Shakespeare's most formally stylized scenes, where three men sit on mounds on the same battlefield: King Henry (lamenting), a soldier who discovers he has killed his own father, and another who discovers he has killed his own son. Richmond's lines here close the loop: that emblematic horror is now over. The anaphora ('The brother... The father... The son...') follows classical rhetorical doctrine (Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 9.3.30: anaphora as 'the repetition of the same word at the beginning of successive clauses'), and is the standard device for enumerating accumulated grievances before a resolution.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Genesis 4:8-11 (Geneva 1599): Cain slays Abel — the archetypal brother-killing whose shadow falls on Richmond's 'brother blindly shed the brother's blood.'

sources.name: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria
sources.citation: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 9.3.30 (c. 95 CE): anaphora defined as beginning successive clauses with the same word, used for rhetorical amplification.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3640

Geneva Bible Genesis 4:8-11 is a real passage attesting Cain's fratricide; Quintilian Institutio Oratoria 9.3.30 genuinely describes the figure of repeating the same word at the start of successive clauses (though Quintilian does not name it 'anaphora' there), and the section number is confirmed by Perseus.

The anaphora identification and the cross-reference to 3 Henry VI 2.5 are both correct, but calling the Cain-and-Abel echo 'deliberate' overstates the textual evidence — the lines invoke fraternal bloodshed generically and no explicit Cain marker is present in this passage; the allusion is plausible but not certain.

anchor_text: Richmond and Elizabeth, The true succeeders of each royal house, By God's fair ordinance conjoin together
summary: Richmond declares himself the Lancastrian heir and Elizabeth of York the Yorkist heir, so their marriage will unite both dynastic claims in one bloodline. 'God's fair ordinance' frames the union not as a political deal but as divine will — the providential design that has been building across Shakespeare's eight history plays. Their descendants were the Tudor monarchs, including Queen Elizabeth I, on the throne when this play was first performed.
detail: The 'Tudor myth,' as historians call it, is the providential reading of the Wars of the Roses promoted by Edward Hall (Union, 1548) and absorbed by Holinshed and Shakespeare: the deposition of Richard II in 1399 was a sin against God's anointed king; the subsequent civil wars were God's punishment; Henry VII's victory and marriage were the divinely appointed resolution. Shakespeare's Richmond is deliberately thin as a character — he functions as an agent of Providence, not a person with doubts or ambitions of his own. Elizabeth of York (daughter of Edward IV, sister of the princes in the Tower) brought the Yorkist legitimacy; Richmond's Lancastrian claim was itself slender (descent through an illegitimate Beaufort line), which is why the providential warrant matters so much to Tudor propaganda. Their son Henry VIII and granddaughter Elizabeth I are the audience's own dynasty.

sources.name: Hall, Union (1548)
sources.citation: Hall, E. The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548): the entire book is structured around the providential arc from Richard II's deposition to Henry VII's union of the roses.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Holinshed, R. Chronicles (1587), vol. 3, 'Richard III': Richmond's closing speech closely follows Hall's providential framing.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3645

Hall's Union (1548) is explicitly structured around the providential arc from Richard II's deposition to Henry VII's union of the roses, and Holinshed (1587) follows Hall's framing; both citations are real and directly support the Tudor-myth claim.

The Tudor-myth reading (Providence resolving the Lancastrian/Yorkist conflict through Henry VII's marriage) is the standard scholarly account deriving from Hall and Holinshed, and the characterisation of Richmond as an agent of Providence rather than a fully individualised character is mainstream; the note about the Beaufort line being slender is accurate.

anchor_text: Abate the edge of traitors, gracious Lord, That would reduce these bloody days again
summary: 'Abate' means blunt or diminish — here, take the cutting edge off traitors, i.e. disarm or weaken anyone who would revive civil war. 'Reduce' does not mean 'lessen' in the modern sense but 'bring back' or 'restore' (from Latin reducere, to lead back). Richmond is praying that God will weaken any traitors who might try to bring England back to the bloodshed just ended.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'abate' v., sense 7: 'To put down, quell, suppress (a person or thing)'; and s.v. 'reduce' v., sense I.1.a: 'To bring back, restore (to a former state or condition).'

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon, 3rd ed. (1902), s.v. 'abate': 'to diminish, lessen, weaken'; s.v. 'reduce': 'to bring back.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3651

OED senses for 'abate' (put down, suppress) and 'reduce' (bring back, restore to a former state) are genuine documented senses, and Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference attesting the same archaic meanings.

Both lexical glosses are correct: OED documents 'abate' in the sense of blunting or quelling and 'reduce' in the Latin-rooted sense of 'bring back / restore,' and both usages are standard in early-modern English.
